#5765. Risk and Reward Along Africa’s Red Sea Littoral

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

Essay: Risk and Reward Along Africa’s Red Sea Littoral

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

The new era of maritime chokepoint disruption has, in many ways, highlighted the importance of Africa’s Red Sea and Gulf of Aden states. The Houthis’ ability to hold the Bab el-Mandeb at risk, combined with the deepening rivalry between the Abraham and Mecca blocs of the Middle East, have created powerful incentives for a range of extra-regional actors to further expand their partnerships along the Horn of Africa’s coastline. This is particularly clear in the southern Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, where the United Arab Emirates, Israel, and the United States have grown their diplomatic and military engagement in Puntland and Somaliland, and where the United States has pursued a diplomatic rapprochement with Eritrea.

What does this mean for the Horn of Africa’s littoral states? Although their geographic proximity to what Bruno Macaes called “the strait at the center of the world” has emerged as valuable strategic currency, it is not hard to see how the attempt to coopt Africa’s Red Sea states into one alliance or another could go wrong. The concerns are threefold: that the Horn’s littoral states might become entrapped in conflicts that are not their own; that the intra-Horn rivalries the littoral states are already enmeshed in are made more acute; and that internal governance conditions in the Horn’s states further deteriorate.

The new era of maritime chokepoint disruption has, in many ways, highlighted the importance of Africa’s Red Sea and Gulf of Aden states. The Houthis’ ability to hold the Bab el-Mandeb at risk, combined with the deepening rivalry between the Abraham and Mecca blocs of the Middle East, have created powerful incentives for a range of extra-regional actors to further expand their partnerships along the Horn of Africa’s coastline. This is particularly clear in the southern Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, where the United Arab Emirates, Israel, and the United States have grown their diplomatic and military engagement in Puntland and Somaliland, and where the United States has pursued a diplomatic rapprochement with Eritrea.

What does this mean for the Horn of Africa’s littoral states? Although their geographic proximity to what Bruno Macaes called “the strait at the center of the world” has emerged as valuable strategic currency, it is not hard to see how the attempt to coopt Africa’s Red Sea states into one alliance or another could go wrong. The concerns are threefold: that the Horn’s littoral states might become entrapped in conflicts that are not their own; that the intra-Horn rivalries the littoral states are already enmeshed in are made more acute; and that internal governance conditions in the Horn’s states further deteriorate.

The Horn’s littoral states cannot wish away geography or the incentives that it creates. But they do have room to maneuver. Robust public debate among Horn publics, prudent decision-making from ruling elites, and conscientious engagement from key external partners can ensure that this new chapter of geopolitical centrality does not further destabilize a region that is already at the precipice.

The Horn of Africa has been a critical node since the inauguration of the Suez Canal in 1869. But the intensity with which this fact has been felt has waxed and waned over time. The start of the Yemen War in 2015 initiated another period of growing entanglement between the Horn of Africa and a range of outside powers, each of whom sought a strategic perch near the Red Sea corridor from which to project their security and commercial interests.

But the turmoil in the  Middle East after Oct. 7, 2023, has sharpened this dynamic. Two developments have been particularly consequential. The first is the Houthi campaign to interrupt maritime traffic in the southern Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, with a first wave of attacks beginning in November 2023 and a second wave targeting Saudi shipping starting in the summer of 2026. The second dynamic has been the deepening rivalry between the Abraham and Mecca blocs of the Middle East. Although these respective blocs are not entirely coherent, there are clear divisions over Israel’s increasingly muscular security policy; the Iran crisis; and their respective interventions in conflicts between national governments and subnational armed actors across the region.

In the face of new strategic pressures, several extra-regional actors have sought enhanced access and position in this zone, over and above what they had secured in preceding years. A triumvirate of littoral countries/de-facto states have been immediate targets: Somaliland, Puntland, and Eritrea.

The impact is most apparent in Somaliland. Its economic partnership with the UAE, through the latter’s investment in the Berbera corridor, is long-standing. But this relationship has become increasingly securitized since 2024. The clearest evidence is what transpired at Berbera Airport, which has come under the effective security control of the UAE. Satellite imagery suggests the construction of an adjoining dock and the hardening of the airport’s infrastructure, including the development of underground bunkers that are potentially for ammunition and fuel. Many believe the airport has also become a logistical node in the UAE’s broader military supply network across East Africa, enabling the delivery of weapons to Sudan and Ethiopia.

Israel’s expanding role in Somaliland has run in parallel with the growing Emirati military presence. Israel diplomatically recognized Somaliland in December 2025—making it the first country in the world to do so—and some reports suggest an active Israeli intelligence presence in Berbera and the use of the airport for refueling its jets during the Iran war. Somaliland officials generally do not confirm these reports but acknowledge that an Israeli military presence is an eventual possibility.

A Soviet-made MiG-17 fighter jet, formerly belonging to the Somali Air Force, sits atop the Hargeisa War Memorial monument in Hargeisa, Somaliland, on Oct. 16. Mohamed Ahmed/Reuters

Washington has also joined the club. In the last year, Somaliland has hosted the commanding generals of AFRICOM and SOCAFRICA. A number of U.S. military personnel based at the Baledogle Airfield in Somalia have now been redeployed to Somaliland, prompting one senior Somaliland official to privately quip, “Team Mogadishu has now become Team Hargeisa.” U.S. training opportunities for Somaliland’s security forces appear to have also grown. These developments are still nascent and as such do not yet involve the deployment of critical intelligence, security, and reconnaissance capabilities, but the direction of travel is fairly clear.

The Emirati government’s formula in Puntland has largely tracked its approach to Somaliland. Beginning in the 2010s, the Emirati footprint in the statelet had mostly consisted of a commercial port concession in Bosaso and training Puntland’s Maritime Security Forces. But from 2024 onward, the UAE scaled up its activity in Bosaso, turning an airbase next to the civilian airport into another logistical hub through which weapons, ammunition, and personnel flowed to Emirati allies throughout the Horn. The UAE has also supported Puntland’s 2024-2025 offensive against Islamic State contingents in the region through direct drone strikes. The United States has also directly backed counter-Islamic State military operations, and according to Puntland authorities, agreed in August 2026 to establish a military facility at the same Bosaso airbase that houses an Emirati presence.

Eritrea’s incorporation into this picture looks a bit different. Its external alignments sharply diverge from Somaliland and Puntland, and there is currently no evidence that Eritrea is poised to play host to foreign military facilities. Yet if the past is prologue, then Eritrea could soon find itself housing a more significant military presence. There are unconfirmed reports of the potential for an increased Egyptian presence in the southern port of Assab. Assab served as the logistical fulcrum of Emirati military operations in Yemen, and back in the early 2000s, the Eritrean government lobbied the United States to establish a military base in Eritrea. At the time, Washington declined the Eritrean offer and established its premiere African military base in neighboring Djibouti.

People sail past container ships anchored near the Bab el-Mandeb strait on Aug. 6. AFP via Getty Images

Maritime exigencies in and around the Bab el-Mandeb have now pushed Eritrea higher on the Trump administration’s agenda. While U.S.-Eritrea relations have been relatively poor for more than two decades, Washington allowed a Tigray-related sanctions package targeting the Eritrean government to expire in September 2026. This was a clear bid to enhance relations with Asmara and was tied to a broad, if not clearly defined, sense that Eritrea mattered for Red Sea security. This sanctions removal occurred even though some important U.S. policymakers believed that Eritrea had not really done enough to warrant such action.

Somaliland, Puntland, and Eritrea will probably extract clear strategic rewards from their emerging geopolitical centrality and the related expansion of security partnerships. All three face increasingly acute security dilemmas from what they regard as revanchist neighbors and their respective external backers. All of their national political projects are also at critical junctures: Somaliland is attempting to build momentum for wider recognition; Puntland is maneuvering to protect its autonomy within a Somali federation; and Eritrea is working to fully break its political estrangement from much of the international system. Somaliland and Puntland have even leveraged the good offices of Abu Dhabi and Washington to improve a bilateral relationship long riddled with tension.

People participate in a rally to celebrate the Houthis’ takeover of the strategic port city of Mocha and the Bab el-Mandeb strait in Sana’a, Yemen, on Sept. 11. Mohammed Hamoud/Getty Images

The risks, however, are very real. The first is that these small polities quickly find themselves entrapped in conflicts that are not their own. The concern is most relevant to Somaliland, where the intensification of the Emirati, Israeli, and U.S. security presence is clearest. Though Houthi attacks in the southern Red Sea and Gulf of Aden have had negative economic repercussions on Berbera port, Somaliland’s authorities have no interest in getting involved in a regional war against the Houthis. But they might not have a choice. The Houthis themselves have threatened to strike any Israeli military presence in Somaliland and even hacked the website of Somaliland’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs in early July. If a conflict led to missile or drone strikes on Berbera, it would have a catastrophic impact on trade, government revenue, and oil imports.

There is also a risk that Somaliland’s deepening security engagement with the Abraham bloc alienates it from Saudi Arabia, which is clearly unnerved by the growing security presence of the Emiratis and Israelis in the southern Red Sea. Somaliland’s critical livestock export sector, which provides 80 percent of all export earnings, is oriented toward the Saudi market, meaning it can ill afford to antagonize Riyadh.

Somaliland’s authorities are no doubt hoping to manage the scale and conduct of the foreign military element within its borders, so as to not provoke retaliation from actors they otherwise have few differences with. Although not widely known, when it was negotiating a memorandum of understanding for sea access with Ethiopia in late 2023, Somaliland placed real limitations on an Ethiopian naval presence in its Gulf of Aden shores. This included the denial of a land corridor between the Ethiopian border and naval base, as well as limits on the Ethiopian military’s interactions with local communities and third-party military activity. But does Somaliland have the autonomy to fully constrain what Israel, the UAE, and the United States do within its borders?

The second risk is that external actors’ push for new Red Sea-oriented partnerships might inadvertently fuel escalatory dynamics in the region. This is most evident in the growing tensions between Eritrea and Ethiopia. The scramble for positions along the Horn’s Red Sea littoral has provided landlocked Ethiopia a new set of justifications to press its maritime claims, including to the port of Assab in Eritrea. Ethiopian officials have argued that since the Red Sea and its Horn ports are increasingly contested terrain, an Ethiopian naval presence is the only way to ensure the country’s economic and security interests. They also make the point that if it is legitimate for outside powers to establish military bases along the Red Sea littoral, then it is an equally legitimate course of action for Ethiopia.

A view of U.S. military aircraft at Camp Lemonnier in Djibouti on Jan. 21, 2024. Djibouti sits opposite Yemen, across the Bab el-Mandeb strait, and between Eritrea and Somaliland.Getty Images

At the same time, U.S. sanctions removal, and the growing proximity between Cairo and Asmara, has increased Eritrea’s willingness to risk conflict with its southern neighbor. Indeed, the decision by the TPLF and the Alliance for Survival to launch offensives on Sept. 23, likely with the approval of Asmara, came just six days after the U.S. sanctions regime on Eritrea expired.

Meanwhile, Emirati-Israeli involvement in Somaliland and Puntland has further consolidated Mogadishu’s increasing all-weather alliance with Turkey. President Hassan Sheikh has used Somalia’s growing defense partnerships with Turkey, which has deployed F-16s to the region to fight Al-Shabaab, to put pressure on Somaliland and Puntland. Most recently, this has involved an electronic visa scheme managed by Mogadishu to control the movement of foreign passport holders into Somaliland, and a reported agreement with Ankara to build a military base in Laasqoray, which sits in territory that Somaliland considers its own.

Analysts fear that the renewed conflict could quickly draw in other regional actors.

How Washington bargains away its Africa strategy to other regions.

As a result, the risk of conflict between Mogadishu, Garowe, and even Hargeisa has increased considerably. In July and August, for instance, there were military confrontations between Puntland’s government and the Puntland Security Force, a militia that had increasingly come under the sway of Mogadishu, resulting in the PSF bases in Galkayo and Bosaso being seized by Puntland authorities.

A final risk is related to the core governance questions that will shape the regional security landscape of the Horn in the coming years.

Consider Eritrea, which has been mired in a deep human rights crisis for decades. This has driven hundreds of thousands of its young people abroad and produced deep, if still suppressed, social fissures. The country has no functioning constitution or electoral system, and thus no mechanism for peacefully navigating succession or adjudicating domestic political differences. Its political elite, in power since 1991, is unwilling to cultivate younger leaders or embrace basic economic and political reforms, offering little more than time-worn cliches about the need to defend against sabotage by external enemies.  Unsurprisingly, U.S. sanctions relief engages none of these issues.

In Somaliland and Puntland, the problem is one of political polarization, as deepening external partnerships have widened disagreements between contending political factions. Somaliland’s recognition deal with Israel has drawn internal criticism, including from religious actors, on both moral and strategic grounds. This was particularly true after Hargeisa made the controversial decision to place its embassy in Jerusalem rather than Tel Aviv in July. In Puntland, some opponents of President Saeed Deni believe he is using Emirati patronage to further consolidate his power. In all of these debates and more, fairly explosive clan rivalries lurk just beneath the surface.

Members of the Somaliland Coast Guard participate in a parade in Hargeisa on May 18. Kang-Chun Cheng/AFP via Getty Images

The Horn’s littoral states can navigate the risks associated with their emerging geopolitical centrality. But it will require more than business as usual. The first step is robust public debate about the risks and rewards of external security entanglements, so that all relevant considerations are surfaced. In many ways, Somaliland is ahead of the curve in this regard, a reflection of its relatively strong—although far from perfect—democratic system.

Ruling elites must also prudently assess the costs and benefits of foreign basing and military cooperation. The challenge here is that the democratic deficit in some of these states means that regime security often prevails over public interest. There are also separate questions of state capacity in some of these polities and the fundamental ability of the government to recognize substantive problems and devise responses. Finally, external partners, particularly the United States, must recognize that the transactionalism of the moment will not deliver stability in one of the world’s most essential maritime corridors. The only solution is to encourage better and more accountable governance along Africa’s Red Sea and Gulf of Aden littoral.

This work is supported by the Cross-Border Conflict Evidence, Policy and Trends (XCEPT) research program, funded by UK International Development. The views and opinions expressed are those of the authors and do not necessarily represent those of the U.K. government.

Michael Woldemariam is an associate professor and the Ph.D. program director in the University of Maryland’s School of Public Policy.

Biruk Terrefe is a lecturer in African politics at the University of Bayreuth and a research associate at Oxford’s African Studies Centre.

#5764. Fascism mixed into cringey online content is easy to mock – but no less dangerous

This article was originally published on The Conversation.

Against the backdrop of an unpopular war in Iran, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced on July 15, 2026, that the Pentagon would begin testing male service members 30 and older for low testosterone. That, the department later said, would include assessing symptoms of low testosterone such as âreduced libido, loss of spontaneous morning erections, erectile dysfunction, diminished energy and physical performance, impaired concentration, reduced muscle mass, and depressed mood.â

The combination of aggressive masculinity and militarism with the implications of testing for something like âspontaneous morning erectionsâ as necessary for war fighting is emblematic of the administrationâs tendency to combine fascist ideas and symbols with outright embarrassing messaging, or what I call âcringe fascism.â

For some time thereâs been a contentious debate among writers, historians and public intellectuals over whether Donald Trumpâs presidency could be considered âfascist.â Some have argued that such claims are hyperbolic or inaccurate, while others say it is a useful and accurate ideological label.

Either way, it would be difficult to deny that the Trump administration frequently draws from the well of fascist imagery and symbolism in its official messaging.

And thatâs where the concept of cringe fascism fits in. In online parlance,âcringeâ is a kind of embarrassment by proxy when someone posts something that should be embarrassing but which doesnât seem to be to them.

For their part, members of the Trump administration have relied on language and symbolism that borrows from the fascist or authoritarian playbook while doing so in a way that commenters often mock as patently ridiculous or embarrassing â or cringe.

But the purported silliness of these ideas, as with Hegsethâs testosterone policy, hides a much more serious â and to some critics, fascist â reality. That, moreover, is why the deployment of cringe can be effective: It can generate enthusiasm among conservative voters by trolling the left while reducing deadly serious policy debates to the level of online memes.

As Americans prepare for the midterms and a surely contentious presidential election in 2028, such considerations of Trumpâs authoritarian tendencies are being put to the test. Thatâs especially true as he consistently threatens the integrity of elections, deploys immigration and other federal law enforcement officers on American streets in a highly contested manner, and attempts to target the press and restrict its access.

As a scholar of conspiracy theories, I have been amazed at some of the more blatant efforts to repurpose fascist imagery by members of Trumpâs inner circle.

Consider, for example, the use of ethnonationalist and fascist imagery of âblood and soilâ in sloganeering by the Department of Homeland Security, or encouraging U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement recruits to âDefend the Homeland.â

And then there are the attacks on the press as the âenemy of the people,â echoing past totalitarian leaders, followed by Trumpâs banning of mainstream media from the White House and the launch of Trump TV as the state channel. Critics view such moves to attack and restrict the press as hallmarks of fascist methods.

Borrowing more obviously from fascist tropes was Trump posting on social media a mock-up of a potential new Space Force uniform. The post claimed to draw inspiration from Paul Verhoevenâs âStarship Troopers,â in which the soldiers are deliberately modeled on the fascist aesthetic and ideology of the Nazis.

Alongside the authoritarian and fascist tropes, the Trump administration cannot seem to avoid âcringe.â

Recent examples include the White House tweeting images of Trump as a videogame character on a select screen with sleeveless blue suit and bulging muscles, or sharing an AI parody of the new Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time game with an awkward video of a pixelated Trump running around the White House lawn. Or consider the post depicting Trump as Green Lantern, using his magic ring to raise a spectral border wall, launch a military attack and fix American industry.

On the one hand, the Trump administration seems determined to keep his party in power and enact a transformative MAGA policy agenda. On the other hand, Trump seems incapable of avoiding cringey riffs such as his digressions on menâs bodies in ways that seem strikingly at odds with his tough-guy persona. To see the commander in chief waxing poetic about Ohio Sen. Jon Hustedâs rear feels deeply surreal.

Trumpâs seemingly incongruous comments occur at the same time that the secretary of defense is advocating hypermasculinity in the military through testosterone testing, reflecting a heady mix of masculinity and military supremacy that has long been a hallmark of fascism. Such a policy is also at odds with how the professional military has presented itself under previous administrations.

The mixture of fascist aesthetics with cringe posting underscores the internal contradictions of the Trump administration.

It is difficult to see criticsâ view of Trumpâs second term as âfascistâ when observers get such awkward online displays of silliness. And when official communications from the White House and federal agencies are equal parts tough talk, trolling and cringe, the underlying policies can get lost in the shuffle.

Is is hard to know whether this flood of cringe is always intentional, but it is certainly confusing and hilarious to both Trumpâs supporters and his opponents. But that belies what many critics have decried as authoritarian actions by this administration, and these comparisons with fascism continue to animate public discourse.

Masked ICE agents continue to operate with some legal protections from the White House in their sometimes-deadly efforts to pursue and round up people it broadly accuses of being in the country illegally.

Likewise, the DHS announced that ICE agents could be deployed to polling locations, while the agency has reportedly attempted to get access to voter information to investigate alleged voter fraud through increased surveillance.

The deployment of cringe might seems like a ridiculous, even unconscious, exercise by an administration that â as with the five-day tenure of former press secretary Katie Zacharia shows â regularly exposes itself to derision and satire. Yet thatâs why the use of such a concept can be so strategically effective: It turns potentially deadly serious policy consequences and ideological choices into a game of memes and online gamesmanship.

Matthew N. Hannah, Associate Professor of Rhetoric, Politics and Culture, University of Wisconsin-Madison

#5763. Trump's birthright citizenship restrictions struck down again by DC federal judge he called 'hater'

Fox News legal editor Kerri Urbahn analyzes President Trump's new executive orders targeting birth tourism and birthright citizenship, plus the legal battle with the ACLU and a Texas hospital settlement. Urbahn discusses the constitutional battles ahead.

A DC federal judge, previously dubbed by President Donald Trump as an "anti- Trump Hater," blocked Trump's second attempt to restrict birthright citizenship in a Wednesday ruling.

U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper, who was recently in Trump's crosshairs after ruling against efforts to shut down the Kennedy Center for renovations and add Trump's name to the cultural institution, issued a 67-page ruling striking down an August executive order that barred U.S. -born children whose parents are suspected terrorists or gang members, or children born through surrogacy to foreign parents, from citizenship eligibility.

Cooper's ruling comes months after the Supreme Court struck down Trump's initial executive order, signed on his first day back in office. The order attempted to deny birthright citizenship to U.S.-born children whose mothers were in the country illegally or temporarily and whose fathers were neither U.S. citizens nor green card holders.

WHITE HOUSE RIPS ‘ACTIVIST’ BIDEN JUDGE WHO UPENDED TRUMP BIRTHRIGHT CITIZENSHIP ORDER

Demonstrators hold up an anti-Trump sign outside the U.S. Supreme Court in Washington, DC, on June 27, 2025, after the justices curbed nationwide injunctions in a case stemming from President Donald Trump's initial bid to end birthright citizenship. (ALEX WROBLEWSKI/AFP via Getty Images)

"As the Supreme Court has made clear, however, the President cannot carve out new exceptions to birthright citizenship for children born within the United States and subject to its laws," Cooper ruled.

Trump's second executive order was already partially blocked on Sept. 2 by U.S. District Judge Deborah Boardman in Maryland, whose injunction protected U.S.-born children of mothers who were in the country illegally or temporarily and whose fathers were neither U.S. citizens nor lawful permanent residents.

Cooper's ruling expanded protections beyond that class to include additional children born to certain foreign government and international organization employees, parents deemed "alien enemies" by the administration and foreign parents who used commercial surrogacy services in the U.S.

"The merits in this case are clear-cut. The Supreme Court has twice confirmed that all children born in this country are U.S. citizens, save only for the small handful who are not subject to U.S. law," Cooper wrote.

In addition to the Supreme Court's June ruling in Trump v. Barbara, Cooper referred to the high court's ruling in United States v. Wong Kim Ark, which determined that a man born to Chinese immigrants was a protected U.S. citizen under the 14th Amendment.

SEN ERIC SCHMITT SEEKS TO END BIRTH TOURISM, REVOKE CITIZENSHIP FOR BABIES OF FOREIGN DIPLOMATS

President Donald Trump speaks during a news conference in the James S. Brady Briefing Room at the White House in Washington, DC, on June 27, 2025, following a U.S. Supreme Court ruling on nationwide injunctions in litigation over his first birthright citizenship executive order. (Mehmet Eser/Middle East Images via AFP)

Cooper noted that Wong Kim Ark established narrow exceptions to birthright citizenship, including for children of foreign diplomats, children born aboard foreign public ships and children of enemy forces occupying American territory.

"While the Fourteenth Amendment may theoretically permit new exceptions beyond those listed in Wong Kim Ark, Congress has not authorized any such exceptions," Cooper wrote.

Cooper argued that membership in a terrorist organization alone does not satisfy the historical exception to birthright citizenship for children of enemy forces occupying U.S. territory. He criticized the Trump administration's contention that foreign invaders could occupy American territory without actually holding it as an "outside-the-box understanding" of what constitutes an occupation.

"To recap, a parent’s purported status as an alien enemy, standing alone, cannot strip a U.S.-born child of his right to birthright citizenship," Cooper wrote. "The alien-enemy exception, properly understood, applies only to children born to hostile enemy forces in temporarily occupied U.S. territory."

Cooper also rejected Trump's attempt to deny birthright citizenship to children born through commercial surrogacy arrangements involving foreign parents, finding that the circumstances of their birth do not exempt them from U.S. jurisdiction.

"Indeed, foreign parents choose surrogacy arrangements in the United States precisely to have the child be governed by U.S. law and have the surrogacy process ‘supervised by a court.," Cooper wrote.

Demonstrators gather outside the U.S. Supreme Court in Washington, DC, on May 15, 2025, in support of birthright citizenship during litigation over President Donald Trump's first executive order narrowing citizenship eligibility for children born on U.S. soil. (Kent Nishimura/Bloomberg via Getty)

He noted that, prior to Trump's second executive order, the State Department recognized the citizenship of children born on American soil regardless of whether they were born through surrogacy.

The Trump administration is expected to appeal the decision and request that the executive order be temporarily enforced while the litigation works its way through the courts, a process that could take months.

"This is just another ruling from an activist judge appointed by Obama attempting to thwart President Trump’s commonsense agenda," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "The birthright citizenship executive order is consistent with the holdings and analysis set forth by the Supreme Court."

The Justice Department could seek temporary relief from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the DC Circuit or seek intervention from the Supreme Court. Fox News Digital reached out to the Justice Department for comment.

In addition to ruling against Trump's Kennedy Center renovation efforts, Cooper ruled that Trump's Department of Government Efficiency must turn over records requested in a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit.

Trump has called Cooper one of the "Radical Left Democrats."

Cooper is also married to Amy Jeffress, who was Biden’s personal lawyer in 2025 and previously did some work for the Jan. 6 committee.

#5761. Democrats call for chip export and AI limits as Huang returns

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., is among Democrats looking to take a harder line on AI and chip exports in the new year. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo)

Incoming Democratic leaders called for tighter semiconductor export controls and investigations of the Trump administration Monday as Nvidia reinstated disgraced CEO Jensen Huang.

The issue also spilled into the party’s Senate majority leader election fight, as Democrats weigh plans to advance bills in the 120th Congress that would regulate artificial intelligence.

The reinstatement of Huang came as President Donald Trump told CNBC on Monday the CEO “did nothing wrong” and that he had been “speaking to the [Nvidia] board directly and indirectly.”

In a Monday statement, Nvidia said its board had “received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., who is challenging Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., for the majority leader role, told reporters Monday that in the “first 100 days” of the new Congress, he wants Senate rules changed to allow for faster floor consideration of bills that had broad bipartisan support in committee.

He also supports legislation to require independent mandatory evaluations of AI systems and updates to liability laws to account not just for harm caused by AI models but for risks of internal development. He also mentioned a bill he sponsored that he said would ensure other electricity consumers don’t bear the costs of data center construction.

Van Hollen also said that Congress should create a special joint committee on AI to consider the technology’s broader impacts, including on the workforce and economy.

“I think we need to move urgently on the safety piece and then move with deliberation, but also speed, on tackling these other issues,” Van Hollen said.

Last week, Sen. John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., wrote to Van Hollen and Schumer proposing a joint committee to “complement” the work of committees of jurisdiction and asking for their plans for AI if they were elected leader.

Speaking to reporters and in his reply to Hickenlooper, Van Hollen also supported greater transparency into the AI industry’s financing and debt structure and tighter export controls on advanced chips like those sold by Nvidia. In particular, he said the Commerce Department should close “loopholes” for remote access to chips and purchase by affiliates of companies banned from directly acquiring sensitive technologies.

Schumer, in a post on X Monday, said Democrats would “work on a bipartisan basis to continue advancing policies that stop the flow of our most powerful technology to the Chinese military and other adversaries.”

“Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain,” Schumer wrote.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., whose caucus officially backed him last week to be speaker in the new year, seconded the need for investigations into Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. He also supported export controls.

“The National Defense Authorization Act must include ironclad export control legislation to prevent powerful AI technology from being exploited by the Chinese Communist Party and other adversaries,” Jeffries wrote, referring to the pending fiscal 2027 defense policy bill.

A manager’s amendment to the Senate’s version of the bill includes several chip export restrictions, including requirements for chip security mechanisms that would allow for verification if semiconductors are diverted to countries of concern and a ban on exporting certain very powerful chips to those countries. The House-passed NDAA does not contain similar language.

Meanwhile, Republican committee leaders pressed forward with plans to bring in Huang for questioning.

Senate Banking Chair Tim Scott, R-S.C., on Monday confirmed plans for a Dec. 3 hearing titled “Protecting America’s AI Advantage: Oversight of U.S. Export Controls” featuring Huang as a witness.

"Mr. Huang’s testimony before the Senate Banking Committee will be critical for protecting America’s AI advantage,” Scott said in a statement. “The national security concerns and adherence to export controls will be central to the committee’s oversight and the congressional hearing."

Scott previously invited Lutnick to testify before the committee on Dec. 10.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., who looks likely to hold the banking gavel next Congress, said Huang’s return as CEO “only increases the urgency” of export controls.

“The reckless decision to bring Jensen Huang back as CEO does not change the fact that Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and the company’s board still owe Congress answers about the company’s compliance with U.S. export controls,” Warren said in a statement.

House Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast, R-Fla., said in a social media video on Monday that Huang and Nvidia’s general counsel Tim Teter would sit for transcribed interviews with his committee and with the House Intelligence Committee and Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party the week of Nov. 30.

The committees also requested that Commerce Undersecretary for Industry and Security Jeffrey Kessler appear before the panels.

John T. Bennett contributed to this report.

#5760. The petty joy of a blue election night

Ten years ago, watching the dawning of the Trump era on Fox News felt appropriate somehow. Notice that I didn’t say it felt right; after all, we were sinking into an anti-Enlightenment Age propped up by Rupert Murdoch’s propaganda machine. Nothing about any of that felt right.

Still, once the phrase “President-elect Donald Trump” became as inevitable as Thanos, and Fox’s anchors giggled like ascendant supervillains, staring into that snarling maw seemed like the responsible thing to do.

Training my focus on CNN and MS NOW in time to catch 2026’s predicted blue wave promised to be just as illuminating. Back in 2016, while everyone else on CNN struggled to make sense of what was happening, commentator Van Jones somberly characterized the results as “whitelash against a changing country.”

Shortly after Trump was inaugurated, he turned against CNN full force, branding it and every other outlet denying favorable coverage as fake news. Trump’s 2024 victory further endangered any media outlets outside of the right-wing echo chamber, as he hit news organizations with obscenely ridiculous legal complaints to force them to bend the knee.

So we’ll pardon Jones for his deliciously petty reaction to what Jake Tapper, the emcee of CNN’s “Election Night in America” telecast, awkwardly described as a “blue-nami.” By the time the Democrats took control of the House and Senate, the previously funereal Anderson Cooper was gleefully eager to hear what Jones had to say. And his colleague did not disappoint, delivering what may have been the night’s most satisfying monologue.

“If you join a cult, at some point the cult leader takes you to Jonestown and tries to get you to drink the Kool-Aid,” he observed as chastened GOP pundit Scott Jennings sat inches away. “This is Jonestown for the Republican Party. They drank the Kool-Aid, and they have candidates that are dropping like flies across the country because they did not stand up to this guy when he was doing things that were wrong . . .

“You join a cult, at some point, you go to Jonestown,” Jones repeated in closing. “That’s where you are tonight, Republicans.” Then he pretended to pass a cup to his Trumpian counterpart.

Election night news coverage is a stressful affair in the best of times. In 2026, CNN and MS NOW, the channel formerly known as MSNBC, entered the fray as battered underdogs. MS NOW is now owned by Versant, a group of cable channels spun off from NBCUniversal. CNN, part of Warner Bros. Discovery, will soon be owned by Skydance and its Trump-allied owner David Ellison.

Neither newsroom can claim relief over what’s on the horizon, which is why Cooper led CNN’s coverage with the air of an undertaker greeting democracy’s mourners. America’s major news outlets have been taking it on the chin with the rest of us — including Cooper, a former “60 Minutes” correspondent who fled Bari Weiss’ CBS takeover only for Ellison to come for his cable news shire anyway. Blue wave or not, CNN’s future is uncertain.

So although MS NOW may be scrappier and looser these days, at least its reporters and pundits aren’t working through an institutional existential crisis. That fatigue showed up in how CNN’s Magic Wall wrangler, John King, lived cautiously from moment to moment, allowing only a mild display of wonder as he shifted between the largely scarlet 2024 map and the much bluer 2026 version.

“What’s happening right now?” King wondered. “What’s the right word? Is it a rebuke? Is it repudiation? Is it shellacking? Is it a spanking? I mean, at the moment, this is the collapse of the president’s party on live television as you watch it play out.”

And for the first time in a decade of watching election nights, it was a joy to experience — like learning how to hope again.

Peddling optimism isn’t the job of any journalistic organization, of course. But knowing what CNN’s newsroom is contending with regardless of this election outcome makes their composure especially admirable. The CNN team had a 10-ton weight pressing down on them and still managed to convey the sense of celebration presumably gripping most of its viewers.

Most people tune out election night noise regardless of whether the vote goes in their favor, perhaps gleaning what they can from the flashy graphics and chyrons. This gave MS NOW’s Ali Velshi an advantage at the network’s Big Board now that his former co-worker Steve Kornacki has moved over to NBC. Both have earned fandoms by injecting levity into managing each election’s data flood.  On Tuesday night, Kornacki inspired a meme simply by being captured on his new network’s Kornacki Cam as he walked down a hall.

But Velshi kept his version of his predecessor’s two-step going, buzzing around on MS NOW’s Big Board with a hummingbird’s energy. “Annie Andrews is outperforming, and Darlene Graham is underperforming,” he rapidly blurted, breaking down the Democratic challenger’s road to her unexpected win in South Carolina over the late Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham’s sister, before turning to the camera with a delightfully bemused look to say, “This is a totally weird conversation that we are having. Right?” It’s true. After years of polls overstating the Democrats’ chances, it did feel strange to have underestimated how much they’d win.

Still, Rachel Maddow‘s ebullience from the moment MS NOW’s coverage began was tough to beat. Before a single result came in, she cheerfully offered, “So far, the one thing we can definitively say is that Americans like our democracy, and they are enjoying using it in record numbers in this cycle.”

Once Democrats claimed majorities in the House and Senate a few hours later, she let loose. In calling the race for Pennsylvania’s 8th congressional district for Democratic Scranton Mayor Paige Cognetti, Maddow couldn’t resist calling her Republican opponent, Rob Bresnahan, a “sometime ghost hunter” as her colleagues snickered in the background.

This is an understandable reaction to voters’ referendum on the president’s unpopular and economically detrimental policies. Americans, regardless of partisan stance, are struggling to afford the basics. But as Chris Hayes pointed to the shock of so many Democratic upsets, he noted that high prices aren’t the only thing forcing this drastic change. “The rot that is coming from the top of the country is very, very, very clearly on voters’ minds,” he said.

So if Jones wants to indulge in a little grave dancing, so be it.

It was even better to see other correspondents take stock of all the history made on Tuesday night. New Hampshire voters chose a Democrat, Chris Pappas, to join the U.S. Senate, making him the first out gay man elected to the chamber.

Voters turned Texas blue and elected four Black governors – including former Atlanta mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms, who became the first woman and the first Black person to be elected governor in Georgia, and the first female Black governor in our country’s history.

Once that state’s contest for governor was called for Bottoms, MS NOW’s team tapped Symone Sanders-Townsend to contextualize what that meant for voters and Black women. Sanders-Townsend reminded us that when Trump calls Georgia to gripe, it will be Bottoms on the other end of the line. She’ll also be the one to ensure the 2028 election is certified for the rightful winner.

But when Sanders-Townsend’s colleagues asked her to share how Bottoms’ victory made her feel, her reaction hit home. “After the 2024 presidential election, for myself and Black women all over this country, it felt like a repudiation of us,” she said, holding back tears. “…There were Black women, myself included, that felt like, ‘Well, maybe America just does not want us.'”

So to Sanders-Townsend, and all the other Black women disappointed by their fellow citizens in 2024, Bottoms’ victory said, “Georgia wanted Keisha.”

That moment didn’t diminish Jones’ take on what this election night meant to him. “This is like Christmas and a birthday and an Easter bunny and Halloween!” he said. “This is the repudiation of Trumpism that people have been hoping for, seeing American democracy stand up.”

But by allowing herself to cry on camera, Sanders-Townsend broadcast a different kind of signal. She let us know that on this night, and for the first time in a long time, it was OK to ease into some sense of relief. And that’s better than the fleeting pleasure of retaliatory pettiness, well-earned though it may be.

#5759. Europe Steps Into the Breach on Ukraine

Analysis: Europe Steps Into the Breach on Ukraine

Understanding the conflict four years in.

Now that the Trump administration appears to have turned unequivocally against Kyiv and in favor of Moscow, it falls to Europe to backstop Ukraine’s survival. This week will be crucial, with the European Council meeting on Nov. 26-27 to decide on an additional loan of 45 billion euros (about $49.5 billion) to tide Ukraine over next year as it wrestles with nonstop missile strikes, jet-powered drones, and a gaping hole in its budget.

The Trump administration has, since the start of its second term, been implacably hostile to Kyiv, from Oval Office beatdowns to a relaxation of sanctions on Russia to demands that Ukraine desist from carrying out long-range strikes against Russian oil facilities. That hostility, like the war, has only escalated, with U.S. President Donald Trump suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports (in a bid to lower fuel prices) and neutering the latest legislation meant to economically punish Moscow.

Now that the Trump administration appears to have turned unequivocally against Kyiv and in favor of Moscow, it falls to Europe to backstop Ukraine’s survival. This week will be crucial, with the European Council meeting on Nov. 26-27 to decide on an additional loan of 45 billion euros (about $49.5 billion) to tide Ukraine over next year as it wrestles with nonstop missile strikes, jet-powered drones, and a gaping hole in its budget.

The Trump administration has, since the start of its second term, been implacably hostile to Kyiv, from Oval Office beatdowns to a relaxation of sanctions on Russia to demands that Ukraine desist from carrying out long-range strikes against Russian oil facilities. That hostility, like the war, has only escalated, with U.S. President Donald Trump suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports (in a bid to lower fuel prices) and neutering the latest legislation meant to economically punish Moscow.

“It began with the diesel deal. This is the longest sustained effort by Team Trump” to put its thumb on the scales, said John Herbst, a former U.S. ambassador to Ukraine. “It annoys me even more that they are helping [Russian President Vladimir] Putin do this. Putin wants to undermine NATO, and that is why it is so frustrating.”

Trump had previously adumbrated his approach to Ukraine by delaying approval of the bipartisan legislation, championed by former Sen. Lindsey Graham, that would have levied stiff tariffs on Russia’s trading partners and put additional sanctions on top Russian officials. When the legislation finally did pass, Trump watered it down, waiving the sanctions and for once forgetting about tariffs.

“I found U.S. policy over the last six weeks depressing,” said Steven Pifer, another former U.S. ambassador to Ukraine. “I think Trump is lost to the cause, even if the American people are not.”

Now it falls to Europe to fill the gap, both in terms of Kyiv’s budget and its defense needs. About half of the new loan is earmarked for Ukraine’s administration and the other half for defense procurement.

The European loan is not a done deal. There are four holdouts among the usual suspects—Hungary, Slovakia, Bulgaria, and the Czech Republic—that are leery of signing onto more blocwide debt to support a country they view askance. But by Friday, informed observers say, the European Union will probably be able to hammer through a fresh 45 billion on top of the 90 billion euro loan for Ukraine that it is still doling out.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has said the latest loan would be backed by frozen Russian assets held in Europe. Those central bank assets total about $300 billion worldwide, with just over $200 billion in Belgium. Despite years of posturing, four years into the war, neither Europe nor the United States nor the United Kingdom has moved from freezing to seizing, fearful of the potential legal, financial, and other consequences of grabbing illicit Russian money. That makes the ultimate collateral for this new European loan something of a question mark.

“Europe has no choice but to fund Ukraine’s defense. The question is how you do it,” said Timothy Ash, a Russia expert at Chatham House. “I find it incredible, when you put it across like this, which taxpayers should pay for this: Europe’s or Russia’s?” (He has some thoughts.)

The bigger question is broader. Europe knows that enabling Ukraine to survive the war, or at least avoid a dishonorable peace, is critical to the country’s survival as well as its own. The problem, which has been apparent since January 2025, is that Ukraine and Europe are on their own. The United States has not provided any fresh financial support for Kyiv since Trump came back to office, has at times interrupted intelligence-sharing and satellite links, and continues to block the sale of much-need missile interceptors held in European inventories.

U.S. Undersecretary of Defense Elbridge Colby scolded Ukraine last week for striking Russian oil facilities, arguing that such attacks were ineffective. (Ukraine’s long-range strikes have taken offline about half of Russia’s refinery capacity in recent months, cratered its energy exports, and are leading to lines at gas stations in Russia.) Meanwhile, Russian missiles and drones continue to rain down on Kyiv, Kharkiv, and other major cities.

“Trump is just defending Putin and making it harder for Ukraine to defend itself,” Herbst said.

Germany’s vocal support for mobilizing hundreds of billions of Moscow’s reserves could be a game-changer for Ukraine.

For all the talk of a new world order, the Trump-Xi-Putin meeting produced little of substance.

One question that looms now is whether Europe’s determination to support Ukraine—Europe has already provided nearly 240 billion euros (about $260 billion), far more than the United States or any other country—will push Trump into reprisal mode. He has in the past slapped tariffs on Europe while waiving penalties on Russia. Over the weekend, Trump posted a photo of himself with Putin titled, simply, “My Friend.”

“If Trump wants to go down that route, it might get ugly in Europe, but I don’t think Europe can afford to let Ukraine lose. There is a real understanding in Europe about how high the stakes are for them,” Ash said.

“It will be interesting to see where this goes in terms of the U.S.-EU relationship. This could be a huge crisis. We have to see how far he is willing to take this.”

Keith Johnson is a staff writer at Foreign Policy covering geoeconomics and energy. Bluesky: @kfj-fp.bsky.social X: @KFJ_FP

#5758. Abdul El-Sayed defeats Mike Rogers despite Haley Stevens drama

Democrat Abdul El-Sayed is projected to defeat Republican Mike Rogers for Michigan‘s open U.S. Senate seat, a closely watched race that capped off a massive night for progressives.

The Associated Press called the race shortly after 2 a.m. Wednesday morning with El-Sayed leading by about seven points.

The candidates were competing to replace retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters, whose departure created one of the most consequential open-seat contests of the midterm elections. El-Sayed, a former Detroit health director, campaigned on expanding access to health care and lowering costs, while Rogers, a former congressman and House Intelligence Committee chairman, emphasized manufacturing jobs, tax cuts and his alignment with President Donald Trump.

The race took an unexpected turn just two days before Election Day when Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens, who narrowly lost the party’s August primary to El-Sayed, endorsed Rogers during an appearance at a Detroit church.

The endorsement stunned Michigan Democrats, prompting condemnation from party leaders and resignations among Stevens’ staff. Stevens cited disagreements with El-Sayed over Israel and his campaign’s direction, while Democrats accused her of undermining their nominee in a critical Senate contest.

El-Sayed sought to move past the controversy, urging supporters to focus on voting. His campaign reported raising $2.4 million on Sunday, while Michigan Democratic officials said the endorsement had prompted an increase in volunteers. Rogers, meanwhile, highlighted Stevens’ support in the campaign’s final days.

More than 2.3 million Michigan voters had already cast ballots by Monday, according to The Associated Press, raising questions about how much the late-breaking controversy could influence the outcome.

#5757. Democrats better hope they don’t have another Manchin in their midst

Ever since the Covid-19 pandemic, America has been in a funk. The whole country has seemed to be in a sour mood, unhappy with everything, feeling as if the world has gone off its axis and life is out of balance. The trauma of that experience was probably far deeper and more injurious than we wanted to admit, so we just sort of sleepwalked as events cascaded around us, feeling emotionally distanced and impotent.

We finally woke up and shook it off. For the first time in six years, the American people took back control of their own destiny and issued a stunning, overwhelming rebuke to the Republican Party, which had fallen back into power during that period of national somnolence and took a wrecking ball, figuratively and literally, to the country. America, it seems, decided to save itself.

The historic landslide Democratic victory in Tuesday’s midterms elections is far more thorough than even the most positive polls had indicated. Analysts assured us that while it looked likely the party would gain at least a House majority, the so-called real victory would be if Democrats reduced the margins in red states, which would serve as a warning to Republicans that they had gone too far. Nobody really expected that Democrats would actually win in places like South Carolina, Kansas, Iowa or perhaps even Mississippi, where, as I write this, Democrat Scott Colom has a 43-vote lead over GOP incumbent Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith.

Political polarization was assumed to be set in stone; the GOP’s redistricting gambit and the Supreme Court’s gutting of the Voting Rights Act meant that Democrats could not expect to flip more than a handful of seats, and the party was facing one of the most inauspicious midterm Senate maps in recent memory. At this moment, they are expected to end up with 245 to 255 seats in the House and possibly 55 seats in the Senate, an unthinkable outcome as recently as yesterday morning.

It will be a while before we see the final tally, but the results are so obviously decisive that even Donald Trump cannot fatuously claim that this election was stolen. All the threats against election workers and plans to contest the outcome are empty in the face of such a victory. It is finally, once and for all, clear that the country does not want the insanity and chaos that Trump has wrought.

According to voter polls — formerly known as exit polls — the top issue for voters was the cost of living, as expected. Reversing the tariffs and putting an end to the war with Iran would be the obvious ways to begin to alleviate some of the stress, followed by restoration of funding for healthcare and other vital safety net programs. Rolling back Trump’s tax cuts for the wealthy would go a long way as well. But the president Trump has already promised to be “Mr. Veto,” so the prospect for a new era of bipartisan comity with the White House does not look good.

It’s always possible that congressional Republicans will feel chastised enough that they will work with Democrats to create veto-proof majorities on those issues, but I wouldn’t hold my breath. The best the Democrats can hope for is that Trump decides he needs to do something positive for his legacy besides building his ballroom and renaming the Atlantic Ocean, and he agrees to compromise on something. I wouldn’t hold my breath on that either. But that doesn’t mean Democrats shouldn’t pass the legislation — and make Trump and Republicans block it.

Progress is hard to attain when, to maintain a majority, your coalition must include some who are opposed to it.

As great as it is that Democrats will decisively control both houses of Congress, that big tent brings with it some perennial problems that are likely to manifest themselves again. The red state-blue state divide represents a structural problem that has always been around, and it has been a specific problem for Democrats going back to at least the time of Franklin Roosevelt. Progress is hard to attain when, to maintain a majority, your coalition must include some who are opposed to it. During Roosevelt’s long presidency, the Democratic coalition included powerful southerners who controlled many congressional committees, and they would simply not pass anything that included civil rights or equitable federal programs. By the end of the 1930s, they had successfully joined with northern Republicans to block much of what remained of the New Deal agenda.

Eventually, as we know, most of that bloc migrated to the GOP, but until fairly recently it’s always been a somewhat fluid dynamic with a few conservative states in the heartland, the West, Southwest and even the South that would elect conservative Democrats. In the last Congress, we dealt with West Virginia’s Joe Manchin and Arizona’s Kyrsten Sinema in the Senate, and it was like pulling teeth to get legislation passed as they used their leverage to extract concessions and block progressive initiatives.

In the not too distant past, Sen. Zell Miller, D-Ga., cosponsored tax cuts, supported the Iraq War resolution and even delivered a keynote speech at the 2004 Republican National Convention. Centrist senators Ben Nelson of Nebraska and Joe Lieberman of Connecticut, along with the conservative Blue Dog Caucus in the House, successfully blocked progressive provisions of the Affordable Care Act. There were other so-called mavericks throughout the 1990s and 2000s who would join with the GOP or leverage their position to thwart liberal initiatives.

I only bring this up to remind people that with the addition of these red state legislators will come a whole set of problems. But given the alternative, they are good problems to have. While the pundits have already begun their ritual of handwringing over the possibility of progressives “overreading the mandate,” the reality is that everyone else understands that the most important priority for Democrats, as a now powerful force of opposition, is to put a check on Trump and begin the critically important process of oversight and accountability. One suspects that on this issue there will likely be unity among all the factions. MS NOW reports that their voter poll showed that 90% of voters said that government corruption was a crucial or major factor in their House vote. That also tracks with the findings of a recent Gallup poll. I would say that’s a pretty clear mandate and a good place to start.

Whatever problems await the Democrats, and there will be many, this was the result we have needed ever since Trump first won the presidency 10 years ago. The damage he has caused in this decade of destruction is immeasurable, but maybe, just maybe, we have finally reached the beginning of the end of our long national nightmare, and we can begin the process of renewal and reformation.

#5754. What Did Xi Jinping Get From the Shenzhen Summit?

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

Analysis: What Did Xi Jinping Get From the Shenzhen Summit?

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

A brief summit between the leaders of China, the United States, and Russia was held in Shenzhen, China, on Nov. 19. Critics saw little substantive achievement, arguing that the three had merely taken advantage of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum to meet for a photo opportunity. Some American observers faulted U.S. President Donald Trump in particular for yielding to China and Russia rather than showing leadership.

In my view, the summit, short as it was, did matter. In great-power politics, the format can sometimes matter more than the concrete results. The leaders of the three countries had never sat down together in this format; that they managed to do so says something about the kind of era that we are entering.

A brief summit between the leaders of China, the United States, and Russia was held in Shenzhen, China, on Nov. 19. Critics saw little substantive achievement, arguing that the three had merely taken advantage of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum to meet for a photo opportunity. Some American observers faulted U.S. President Donald Trump in particular for yielding to China and Russia rather than showing leadership.

In my view, the summit, short as it was, did matter. In great-power politics, the format can sometimes matter more than the concrete results. The leaders of the three countries had never sat down together in this format; that they managed to do so says something about the kind of era that we are entering.

In an era of great-power politics, one of the keys to avoiding military conflict is for the powers to hear one another out. They did so in Shenzhen. They also exceeded expectations by issuing a joint peace declaration with four points of agreement. And for Chinese President Xi Jinping in particular, the summit offered a first chance to try out an approach to great-power relations that he had originally proposed to Washington, this time with both the United States and Russia at the table.

Yet while Xi hosted, the biggest winner was clearly Russian President Vladimir Putin. The war in Ukraine has left Russia diplomatically isolated from much of the West. Shenzhen could not end that isolation, but it showed that Russia could not simply be shut out of great-power diplomacy. Russia is a major military power and rich in natural resources, but its overall strength still falls well short of that of the United States or China. By sitting down with Putin as an equal, the Chinese and American leaders acknowledged that Russia remains a power that they cannot bypass on questions of global strategic security.

Xi was a winner, too. Beijing showed that it could bring two adversaries, the United States and Russia, together on Chinese soil and secure a joint declaration. The format itself put China back at the center of the international stage. A decade ago, it would have been hard to imagine China convening such a meeting. That also helped Xi’s standing at home.

Trump had just suffered a crushing defeat in the midterm elections. Yet both China and Russia accorded him the respect due an American president with whom they could still discuss strategic matters. China, in particular, gave him a lavish welcome rather than treating him as a lame duck.

But the three leaders did not sit around a table simply for the sake of appearances, and Xi in particular made some meaningful gains here. The Chinese president raised the question of how the three powers should deal with one another from here on. His answer: with mutual respect, peaceful coexistence, mutually beneficial cooperation, and dialogue and consultation.

These are principles that Beijing has long pressed in its dealings with Washington, rooted in Xi’s proposal for a “new type of great-power relations” between China and the United States. As host, Xi set the tone by extending that framework to all three countries. The summit was a chance for Beijing to put it into practice. In effect, Xi brought Putin into the room to press Trump on an approach that he had long advocated for U.S.-China relations.

That, from Beijing’s perspective, was the summit’s most important achievement. Rivalry between Washington and Beijing, and outright hostility between Washington and Moscow, did not prevent the three countries from coordinating on strategic stability.

This takes a minimum of trust. None of the three countries has to believe that its rivals will give up competing. Each has to believe that the others also want to prevent a miscalculation from triggering a conflict, that they are willing to explain their intentions, and that they will listen when another country spells out its red lines. Sitting down together, rather than meeting only in pairs, means letting down their guard enough to acknowledge that some risks involve all three and cannot necessarily be managed through bilateral talks alone.

If regular coordination takes hold, then Shenzhen will matter even more to Beijing. After the summit, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi said that China would stay in touch with Russia and the United States at the working level. That is a start. Whether the leaders’ dialogue lasts will depend on whether they meet a second or third time, and whether communication holds up when relations come under strain.

Those gains stem largely from the format. The declaration itself offers further clues to what Beijing wanted to accomplish. The first, third, and fourth points are particularly revealing.

The first concerns U.N. reform. The three countries agreed to work toward reforming the United Nations so it could respond more effectively to global challenges and better fulfill its basic mission of maintaining international peace and security.

My reading is that Beijing pushed for this language to reassure the global south. Beijing knows that some countries in the global south are uneasy about China sitting down with the United States and Russia at a summit of its own making. Putting the U.N. reform first sent a related message: The three powers had met to help the United Nations fulfill its peace and security mandate and had no intention of making new rules over the heads of the global south. Wang’s insistence after the summit that countries large and small are equal was meant to convey the same point.

The third point in the declaration names the International Criminal Court. The leaders emphasized the importance of state consent and respect for the immunity of state officials, and they said the court and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction. Moscow likely pushed for this provision in response to the court’s arrest warrant for Putin, backed by Trump due to the U.S. far right’s hostility toward the court. But the words “and other similar bodies” were most likely added at Beijing’s insistence. They give China a joint statement that it can cite in future disputes over jurisdiction, such as the South China Sea arbitration.

Those words also have implications for Taiwan. If mainland China were to attack Taiwan and Washington were to push for Chinese leaders to be held criminally accountable for alleged war crimes, Beijing could point to a declaration the United States helped issue and ask: What did you say in Shenzhen about state consent and the immunity of officials?

The fourth point can be read as a gain for Beijing on nuclear issues. The three countries reaffirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought—language that originated with U.S. President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev, but that has been taken up by China. They also agreed to hold talks on reducing nuclear risks and preventing proliferation.

Trump wanted trilateral nuclear disarmament talks. What made it into the declaration was language on risk reduction and nonproliferation. Beijing succeeded in redirecting U.S. pressure to join disarmament talks toward issues that all three countries might be willing to keep discussing.

China also gained a basis for putting diplomatic pressure on Japan, where changes to—or even the abandonment of—the three non-nuclear principles are under consideration. If Tokyo goes down that path, particularly if the debate turns to Japan acquiring nuclear weapons of its own, Beijing can cite the trilateral agreement and press Washington to say where it stands on those risks.

Xi showed at Shenzhen that China could convene two adversaries, set a framework for discussing strategic stability, and get them to agree on some common positions. As much criticism as the meeting drew, it also raised hopes that trilateral talks might become a regular fixture. Xi’s remarks suggest that he would like to see that happen. The real test will come when the three countries face a crisis and their interests collide. Will they still be willing to talk the way that they did in Shenzhen?

Deng Yuwen is a Chinese writer and scholar.

#5753. Texas Republicans’ gerrymander backfires as Democrats gain ground in U.S. House delegation

This article originally appeared on The Texas Tribune.

In 2025, Texas Republicans, pushed by President Donald Trump, redrew the state’s congressional map before the midterms, converting five Democratic-held districts into ones Trump would have carried by at least 10 percentage points.

The move backfired: GOP candidates lost four of five seats their new congressional map was designed to flip and lost two of their own.

That means Texas Republicans will head to Washington in January with 24 U.S. House seats, one less than they had at the start of the current Congress. When the state Legislature in Austin pursued the controversial mid-decade gerrymander, Republicans had hoped for a 30-8 split in the delegation but will end up instead at 24-14.

In South Texas, moderate Democratic Reps. Henry Cuellar of Laredo and Vicente Gonzalez of McAllen both won reelection, surviving the redraw that put more Trump voters in their districts. Republicans also lost ground in the lone Rio Grande Valley district they already held, as Tejano musician Bobby Pulido ousted two-term Rep. Monica De La Cruz, R-Edinburg.

Democrats picked up another seat with Katy Padilla Stout’s win over YouTuber and gun-rights activist Brandon Herrera in the 23rd Congressional District, a sprawling seat covering San Antonio to the outskirts of El Paso. The district has been vacant since former GOP Rep. Tony Gonzales resigned in April over a sex scandal with a staffer. Despite the district’s 15-point lean for Trump, Padilla Stout, a San Antonio attorney and former teacher, made it onto the radar of national Democrats who saw opportunity in the district’s majority-Hispanic status and Herrera’s history of edgy, controversial comments.

Democrats held fast to districts elsewhere, despite their incumbents being displaced due to the redraw. In the San Antonio area, Bexar County sheriff’s deputy Johnny Garcia beat Republican Carlos De La Cruz, the brother of Monica De La Cruz, in the newly crafted 35th Congressional District, a GOP target that Trump carried by 10 points.

In Houston, the grassroots campaign of Democrat Leticia Gutierrez topped Army veteran and former investment banker Alex Mealer, despite being vastly outspent in a district that Trump won by 20 percentage points two years ago. Gutierrez raised just a fraction of Mealer’s $2.8 million haul over the midterm cycle, as of mid-October, according to Federal Election Commission filings.

Republicans had high hopes for the redraw, which Democrats fought by fleeing the state, keeping the map in limbo by temporarily denying Republicans the headcount to pass it. But the new lines could not withstand the blue wave that swept through much of the country Tuesday, driven in part by the leftward swing of Latino voters. Texas’ new map banked on the GOP holding most of Trump’s 2024 gains with Latino Texans, who made up a majority of the eligible voting population in four of the five targets.

Nor did the redraw deliver what the White House wanted from it: a buffer that would preserve Republicans’ slim U.S. House majority. Trump’s push for the Texas map kicked off a tit-for-tat redistricting war across the country, producing similarly skewed maps in a number of states.

After Texas, Republicans were most hopeful to flip four Democratic seats they redrew in Florida. Three of them stayed blue, and the other was within a one-point margin. In California, where Democrats retaliated with new congressional maps of their own, they had picked up three of the five they targeted and were leading in the remaining two.

With GOP-leaning congressional maps powerless in the face of the blue wave, Democrats won the U.S. House and are set to have a substantial majority.The party has also wrested control of the U.S. Senate, leaving Trump to reckon with a Congress under full Democratic control for his last two years in office.

Under less dramatic circumstances, a number of new faces will join the ranks of Texas’ congressional delegation to replace ten U.S. representatives who are either retiring, gave up their seats to run for other offices or lost their primaries for reelection. Most of the races were in noncompetitive general election districts.

Two sitting representatives ran for U.S. Senate but lost in their respective primaries: Rep. Jasmine Crockett, D-Dallas, fell to James Talarico while GOP Rep. Wesley Hunt, R-Houston, finished behind Sen. John Cornyn and Ken Paxton.

Reverend Frederick Haynes III won Crockett’s endorsement to succeed her in the heavily Democratic 30th District. A Dallas native, Haynes has been pastor of the city’s Friendship-West Baptist Church for more than 40 years. He sailed his way into Congress in the deep blue district Tuesday.

Mortgage loan officer Jon Bonck will succeed Hunt in the safely red 38th District. Bonck received endorsements from Trump, Sen. Ted Cruz and other influential Republicans leading up to his victory in the general election.

The tenure of Rep. Chip Roy will also come to an end in January after the congressman ran for Texas attorney general, a contest he lost in a primary runoff to Mayes Middleton. This election left the staunchly Republican 21st District in the hands of Mark Teixeira, a former professional baseball player who started his 14-season Major League career as the fifth overall draft pick for the Texas Rangers in 2001.

And one incumbent, Rep. Dan Crenshaw, was forced into an early exit from his safe Republican seat by his primary rival, state Rep. Steve Toth of Conroe. The business owner defeated investment banker and Democratic nominee Shaun Finnie, and will be joining the U.S. House after five total terms, including the last eight years, as a state legislator.

Among the six soon-to-be retirees, two are Democrats. The seats of Reps. Lloyd Doggett and Marc Veasey will be filled, respectively, by Rep. Greg Casar, who ran for Doggett’s Austin seat after his own district was scrambled, and former Rep. Colin Allred. Both are returning to Congress — Allred after two years out of office — in new districts.

A new cast of Republicans will take over in four other safe districts.

Five-term Rep. Jodey Arrington will leave his seat to Tom Sell, who worked in the office of former Rep. Larry Combest. Sell worked at a law firm he founded with Combest before running for the U.S. House.

Rep. Michael McCaul will be succeeded by Chris Gober, who, before running for office, worked as the chief lawyer of Elon Musk’s America PAC that has channeled $216 million toward Republicans this cycle.

Rep. Morgan Luttrell also chose not to run for reelection after two terms. That opened the door for Jessica Steinmann, an attorney who previously worked in Cruz’s office as well as in the first Trump administration’s Department of Justice.

And a deceptively familiar face will replace Rep. Troy Nehls – that of his identical twin brother, Trever Nehls, who served in the U.S. Army for more than three decades and retired from the military as a Colonel. He’ll represent the Houston-area 22nd Congressional District.

This article first appeared on The Texas Tribune.
