Get audio access with any FP subscription.

A World for All begins with a foreword from Sen. Bernie Sanders—who, being Bernie Sanders, does not pull any punches. U.S. foreign policy, he declares, has been “plagued by militarism, corporate power, and the selective application of international law.” His solution? The “United States should be pro­moting peace, not endless war,” he suggests, as well as the principle of “enlightened self-interest.”

What’s striking about the foreign-policy debate within the Democratic Party right now is that almost everyone involved would agree with Sanders’ statements. But where more traditional Democrats believe this critique applies mostly to Republicans, many progressives would apply it with equal vehemence to Democratic foreign policy as well. And where one side largely believes that the Barack Obama and Joe Biden administrations tried, however imperfectly, to advance these goals amid a host of challenges, the other believes they could have done much more.

A World for All begins with a foreword from Sen. Bernie Sanders—who, being Bernie Sanders, does not pull any punches. U.S. foreign policy, he declares, has been “plagued by militarism, corporate power, and the selective application of international law.” His solution? The “United States should be pro­moting peace, not endless war,” he suggests, as well as the principle of “enlightened self-interest.”

A World for All: New Visions of U.S. Foreign Policy, ed. Matt Duss, OR Books, 288 pp., $19.95, November 2026

What’s striking about the foreign-policy debate within the Democratic Party right now is that almost everyone involved would agree with Sanders’ statements. But where more traditional Democrats believe this critique applies mostly to Republicans, many progressives would apply it with equal vehemence to Democratic foreign policy as well. And where one side largely believes that the Barack Obama and Joe Biden administrations tried, however imperfectly, to advance these goals amid a host of challenges, the other believes they could have done much more.

A World for All, edited by Matt Duss (who previously served as a foreign-policy advisor to Sanders), bills itself as a “progressive blueprint” for U.S. foreign policy. It consists of 18 chapters, all written by different authors from the academic and think tank community covering a wide range of foreign-policy topics. At a time when a small but vocal group of Moscow apologists and Hamas enthusiasts has tried to put their stamp on the movement, this book shows that many thoughtful and principled voices still dominate progressive foreign-policy thinking. And as interest grows in the Democratic agenda after the midterms’ blue wave, it also serves as a welcome reminder of how much the entire party has in common when it comes to foreign policy.

Children wave flags and flowers as Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin attend a ceremony in Beijing on May 20.Maxim Shemetov/China Pool via Getty Images

Russia, China, and the Middle East: If there are three areas where Washington struggles in pursuing peace, it is these. So what do the contributors to A World for All propose?

The greatest continuity appears in the case of Russia. Here, Michael Kimmage, a Cold War historian, suggests four pillars for U.S. policy:

[M]aintaining and expanding meaningful channels of communication with Russia geared toward desired de-confliction and the avoidance of escalatory spirals; aiding Ukraine and containing Russian military power in Europe; monitoring Russia’s global activities and resisting them in a restrained and targeted, not reflexive or messianic fashion; and keeping an open mind as to Russia’s future.

It is hard to imagine most Biden officials finding anything here to disagree with. In fact, they might only object to the extent that this framing implies Biden himself was being reflexive, messianic, or close minded about Russia’s future.

The reason for this congruity, of course, is that the biggest obstacle to a cooperative relationship with Russia is Russia itself. As Kimmage writes, Washington “has been unable to find an enduring partnership, and it has been repeatedly surprised by aggressive Russian acts, from the invasion of Georgia in 2008 to the massive invasion of Ukraine in 2022.”

He might have added that U.S. President George W. Bush initially sought to work with Russian President Vladimir Putin in the so-called war on terror, or that Obama came into office in search of his famous “reset” with Russia. But because of Russia’s actions, even progressives are now considerably more pessimistic about the possibility of a better relationship with Moscow than both their Republican and Democratic predecessors.

In the case of China, think-tankers Jake Werner and Sandy Shan offer a more pointed contrast with Biden’s approach. With the aim of building a more cooperative relationship with Beijing, they call for the next administration to “[s]et a course to ending economic warfare against China” and normalizing “the presence of China in the US economy.” The two powers, they argue, must work together to “reform global economic governance” and “advance global climate action.”

Call them the restrainers, the riders, and the racers.

Meet the potential foreign-policy and national security big hitters of the next Congress.

The difference in their recommendations appears less in the stated goals than in what compromises a new president might make to achieve them. In responding to previous progressive critiques along the same lines, several former Biden officials have insisted that they too sought a cooperative relationship, but the problem came from Beijing. For example, Thomas Wright, who was on Biden’s National Security Council, argued in the Atlantic in July:

Biden did seek to cooperate with China on issues of mutual concern, such as AI. But he insisted that this had to be done without preconditions. That’s because those of us who worked on these policies inside the administration knew the Chinese playbook well. Beijing had little interest in cooperating on climate or anything else. It would stall by demanding that the U.S. make a concession on some matter of strategic importance, such as Taiwan and export controls.

While export controls or other economic measures might not be a concern for Werner and Shan, it is harder to tell how they think progressives should respond to demands for concessions on issues such as Taiwan. Here A World for All seeks to telegraph a different approach without necessarily spelling out the details.

Werner and Shan write that Chinese aggression against Taiwan would be a “cataclysm.” They argue that U.S. “measures to deter Chinese adventurism should therefore continue” but also be “balanced by stronger and more sincere efforts to reas­sure China that the United States is not pursuing permanent sepa­ration.” That is the sole reference to deterring Beijing in the book—which, read alongside repeated criticisms of U.S. militarism and the size of the Pentagon budget, certainly suggests a greatly reduced willingness to go to war in defense of Taiwan. And yet at face value, that line inevitably implies some commitment to using force. The result is nothing if not strategic ambiguity.

Needless to say, it is in the Middle East that the break with traditional Democratic foreign policy is clearest. The Biden administration’s consistent support for Israel’s genocidal policies in Gaza produced the starkest and most emotional division in the party. In the book, analysts Thanassis Cambanis and Zaha Hassan call for Washington to “end blank-check military support for Israel,” which increasingly seems like a demand that Democrats will make of any candidate in 2028.

Elsewhere in this section, though, their recommendations differ from past Democratic administrations more in degree than kind. They call for more diplomacy and fewer reckless wars, as well as supporting human rights over friendly autocrats. More pointedly, they call for reducing Washington’s military footprint in the region to “discourage unreliable partners and allies from starting wars they believe the US will finish for them.”

U.S. Army soldiers watch as Barack Obama is sworn in as the 44th president of the United States at a base near Baghdad on Jan. 20, 2009.Chris Hondros/Getty Images

Rhetorically, at least, these are all ambitions Obama and Biden shared. Obama ran on his opposition to the Iraq War, withdrew U.S. troops from Iraq, and resisted strong pressure to intervene in Syria. He also offered conditional support for the Arab Spring and negotiated a nuclear agreement with Iran, which he hoped would facilitate a “pivot to Asia.” Biden, for his part, campaigned on the promise to restore the Iran deal and make Saudi Arabia “a pariah” for its human rights abuses.

Both men, however, faced constraints in achieving these ambitions. Obama could have done more to push back against the military coup that ended any hope of a democratic transition in Egypt, but this was unlikely to change the ultimate outcome. In a similar vein, Obama was forced to send U.S. troops back to Iraq when the Islamic State upended the region, while Biden ultimately concluded that a fist bump with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman was the price to pay for the cooperation on oil prices he needed to keep his domestic agenda on track.

A more progressive administration is likely to face some of the same contradictions as their predecessors, even if they ultimately resolve them differently. Indeed, the challenge in evaluating this genre of policy writing, progressive or otherwise, is that, in the abstract, everyone wants their strategy to do everything. Whether you propose competing with rival powers while seeking areas of cooperation where possible or, alternatively, pursuing cooperation while competing where necessary, the real differences only emerge in the way policymakers negotiate the inevitable tradeoffs.

Of course, a constructive conversation about the tradeoffs Biden faced would be easier if members of his administration were more candid about where they fell short. So long as former officials continue to defend their record on Gaza, or proffer weak, equivocal, and mealy mouthed apologies, they will only make it harder to draw useful lessons from his tenure in other areas.

U.S. President Joe Biden (left) is welcomed by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, on July 15, 2022. Royal Court of Saudi Arabia/via Getty Images

More broadly, A World for All suggests that progressives, no less than other Democrats, are still struggling with two enduring tensions that will plague any future administration.

First, it is clear to everyone in the party that the health of U.S. democracy is intertwined with the fate of democracy worldwide. Yet the last few decades have also made it clear how limited Washington’s tools for democracy promotion can be. One approach that several authors highlight is a renewed focus on fighting corruption at home and abroad.

Progressives have led the way in insisting that authoritarianism and corruption are inextricably intertwined. A war against kleptocracy would be smart policy and smart politics, and it would certainly represent a concrete step toward making the world safe for democracy. Yet for the same reason, its impact would be limited so long as many of the countries the United States deals with remain authoritarian. Deploying Magnitsky sanctions against corrupt leaders implicated in bribing Americans or facilitating transnational repression is, in itself, an excellent idea. But it is also hard to imagine rebuilding ties with a new Russian government or pursuing a more cooperative relationship with China while simultaneously sanctioning some of their top officials.

U.S. President Donald Trump walks to Marine One at the White House in Washington on Oct. 6.Finn Gomez/Getty Images

The bigger contradiction is that in the very areas where both the traditional Democratic and progressive approaches to foreign policy differ from those of many Republicans—that is, diplomacy, cooperation, and multilateralism—they are uniquely susceptible to the kind of disruption Donald Trump has created. These all depend on trust and continuity, which is exactly what no one should expect from U.S. foreign policy in the coming decades. Among the many challenges Biden faced in restoring the Iran nuclear deal, for example, was Tehran’s demand for some reassurance that Trump would not simply tear it up again if he was reelected. This, of course, was something Biden could not provide and, as events proved, something that Iran was wise to ask for.

In their chapter on Europe, analysts Rachel Rizzo and Max Bergmann offer one clear-eyed example of what confronting this reality could look like. They argue that, rather than simply try to restore the traditional transatlantic relationship rooted in a strong U.S. commitment to NATO, the next administration should support Europe’s efforts to become “a stronger and more assertive global actor” with more independent defense capabilities.

Can Washington hope to find actors abroad who will support U.S. values more reliably than the United States itself? It’s hardly an ideal solution. But then, if Democrats win the presidency in 2028, they will hardly be inheriting an ideal foreign policy situation.

#5707. China Doesn’t Want a Nuclear Arms Race

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

LYLE J. GOLDSTEIN is Director of the Asia Program at Defense Priorities and Director of the China Initiative at Brown University’s Watson School of International and Public Affairs.

NINA TANNENWALD is Associate Teaching Professor of Political Science at Brown University.

How America Can Avert an Unnecessary Rivalry

Today, pessimism—almost fatalism—reigns in Washington about the United States’ ability to avoid a costly and dangerous arms race with China. Policymakers point to China’s increasingly aggressive policies toward Taiwan, its massive military buildup, and its resistance to engaging in some arms control measures as evidence that Beijing has accepted the inevitability of such a race or is even pursuing one. Worried by intellectual frameworks that emphasize the likelihood of war between rival great powers, many U.S. leaders and analysts see little choice but for the United States to arm itself, too. But this thinking risks becoming a self-fulling prophecy. The major danger is that an unrestrained arms race increases the likelihood of war over Taiwan or even of a catastrophic nuclear exchange.

But the pessimism about averting an arms race is misplaced. A nuclear arms race, in particular, is not a foregone conclusion—and the United States has real opportunities to curb one. Avoiding a nuclear arms race will require a broader approach than the two-pronged one Washington has recently favored: building up U.S. nuclear deterrence and seeking to force concessions from Beijing by imposing restrictions on trade and technology transfers. American leaders should instead look beyond traditional deterrence, which falls short because its threat-based approach tends to provoke competition over arms, and strive to establish a more fundamental strategic stability through a process of reciprocal de-escalation and compromise. China is likely to be amenable to reciprocal de-escalation: it has a long tradition of moderation in nuclear matters and, ultimately, Chinese leaders do not want a war over Taiwan.

There are recent signs that even U.S. President Donald Trump, who has often boasted about his distaste for compromise, sees the value of engagement. After two U.S.-Chinese bilateral summits this year, in October he suggested that his November trilateral meeting in Shenzhen with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin should focus on “denuclearization.” But Washington will have to become much more consistent in its rejection of an arms race, including by modifying its support for Taiwan and incorporating China into global arms control leadership. A nuclear arms race with China becomes inevitable only if Washington continues to believe it is.

China is undoubtedly pursuing a military buildup, including investments in nuclear weapons. Between 2020 and 2025, China doubled the number of its nuclear warheads, from 300 to 600—a startling increase, although its arsenal remains small compared with the United States’ approximately 3,700 warheads. In 2021, researchers at the Federation of American Scientists announced that China was constructing 350 new nuclear missile silos in three vast sites in Xinjiang and Gansu provinces. Beijing is also pursuing substantial qualitative upgrades to its nuclear weapons, a push it showcased at an October 2025 military parade that unveiled a new sea-launched ballistic missile, two new kinds of intercontinental ballistic missiles, a new air-launched hypersonic missile, and a new long-range hypersonic cruise missile.

Then, this July, the Chinese navy tested a submarine-launched long-range ballistic missile that could carry nuclear weapons. This significant new capability will allow China to launch long-range nuclear strikes that can reach the United States from protected waters near its own coastline rather than having to sail out into the Pacific. A recent editorial in a leading Chinese foreign affairs newspaper took the candid yet disturbing step of explicitly linking China’s rapid nuclear buildup to its desire to exert sovereignty over Taiwan. “The great cause of national reunification,” it asserted, “must rest on a solid, realistic foundation. That foundation is, first and foremost, hard power.” Although such overt nuclear saber rattling remains rare, the link between Beijing’s nuclear forces and the Taiwan issue stretches back over three decades and is also supported by the scholar Tong Zhao’s detailed analysis of China’s nuclear buildup in Foreign Affairs in May.

As China builds up its military, the perception that it is on a collision course with the United States over Taiwan—one that inevitably includes the risk of nuclear escalation—has become widespread in Washington. Taiwan, of course, appears to be an obvious flash point. The United States has long committed itself informally to defending the island while China seeks to unify with it, by force if necessary. In October, Army General Ronald Clark, the head of the U.S. Pacific Command, affirmed that his forces are actively readying for a Chinese invasion of Taiwan that could come as early as 2027.

The Biden administration and both Trump administrations made some attempts to engage China over arms control and nuclear risk reduction. Trump proposed trilateral arms control talks that would include Russia, whereas the Biden administration pursued bilateral talks with China on strategic stability and nuclear risk reduction. But both presidents gave up after China consistently rejected engaging in sustained talks on nuclear matters. Beijing’s stance is that it has a small nuclear arsenal compared with the United States and Russia and that it is important to first establish trust and mutual reassurance about core interests.

Beyond China’s resistance to arms control, theories about power that are trendy in Washington reinforce the collision course mentality. Numerous realist scholars argue that a U.S.-Chinese rivalry and even a great-power war may be structurally difficult to avoid. The political scientist Graham Allison captured this pessimism in his influential 2017 book, Destined for War, which argued that a so-called Thucydides trap—when a rapidly rising power challenges the position of the dominant power, yielding war—would doom the United States and China to conflict.

China hawks, such as Undersecretary of Defense for Policy Elbridge Colby, increasingly advocate an aggressive focus on “preparing for World War III” with China as a way to avoid it. In a July New York Times interview, Colby argued that the United States must “deny” China “the ability to seize and hold the key territory” of Taiwan, by enhancing U.S. deterrence with a massive military buildup. The next month, speaking at a military conference, Colby specified that such a buildup ought to put a greater emphasis on tactical nuclear weapons and the ability to fight a so-called limited nuclear war. The enemy, Colby said, has “got to believe there’s some sense in which we would use” nuclear weapons. Toward this end, the United States is building a new intercontinental ballistic missile, a new air-launched cruise missile, and new nuclear-armed submarines and bombers, and accelerating the ambitious Golden Dome homeland missile defense project. Unlike earlier U.S. missile defenses, which were designed to intercept limited strikes by so called rogue states such as Iran and North Korea, the Golden Dome is intended to defend against massive Chinese or Russian attacks. But the prospect of losing its ability to retaliate against a U.S. first strike only gives Beijing more incentive to expand its nuclear arsenal.

Such a nuclear-heavy approach only prevents a war with China if nuclear deterrence succeeds. That puts a lot of eggs in the deterrence basket. And recent wars suggest that nuclear deterrence is becoming less effective. Russia’s nuclear threats have not coerced Ukraine into halting its strikes deep into Russian territory. Iran has proved willing to launch strikes against nuclear-armed Israel as well as U.S. bases and allies in the Middle East. What is most ominous, in May 2025, India and Pakistan crossed previous redlines and attacked each other’s homelands, something that mutual nuclear deterrence was supposed to prevent. Even if neither the United States nor China want nuclear war, a China determined to unify with Taiwan may not be intimidated by U.S. nuclear threats.

A recent study by Brown University’s Costs of War program found that the United States has already spent more than $3.4 trillion on its militarized rivalry with China over the last decade. Sustaining or ramping up this spending—which encompasses new warships, aircraft, long-range missiles, drones, base upgrades, forward deployments, large military exercises, research and development, and new nuclear weapons—is infeasible in an era of ballooning national debt and expanding domestic needs.

One of the tragedies of an arms race is that neither party may actually want to pursue one. Despite its current arms buildup, Beijing has a long record of moderation in military and nuclear matters. For many decades, it has maintained a minimal nuclear deterrent and a no-first-use policy, and it did not use major military force to achieve strategic goals. Although it has long had access to the relevant technologies, China appears not to have produced or deployed tactical nuclear weapons. Chinese diplomats played a substantial role in coaxing Iran to accept the Obama administration’s 2015 nuclear deal and supported the UN’s relatively stringent sanctions on North Korea. And in the fall of 2022, according to then Secretary of State Antony Blinken and reporting by the Financial Times, China likely intervened diplomatically with the Kremlin to help stop Russia from using nuclear weapons in Ukraine. More broadly, China has embraced international law when it comes to war, playing a constructive role, for example, in removing chemical weapons from Syria in 2013.

Beijing’s inclination toward restraint has not disappeared completely, even as it upgrades its military. In November 2023, U.S. President Joe Biden and Xi agreed to renew lines of communication between their countries’ militaries that had been severed after U.S. House Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taiwan the previous year. A year later, the two leaders affirmed that humans, not AI, must control the decision to use nuclear weapons. And in late 2025, Beijing released a white paper emphatically reiterating its support for nuclear arms control and has moved toward more transparency by publishing more information, including in English, about its military upgrades.

Chinese leaders clearly do not want a war over Taiwan. Publicly, they repeatedly emphasize that their goal is “peaceful unification” and “winning without fighting,” invoking the Chinese strategist Sun-tzu. Beijing’s longtime “one country, two systems” policy toward Taiwan—which would bring the island under Chinese sovereignty while allowing it substantial autonomy—leaves room for a negotiated solution. Last year, in an important analysis of China’s strategic ambitions, the scholars David Kang, Jackie Wong, and Zenobia Chan examined 12,000 articles and hundreds of speeches by Xi to argue that Beijing prioritizes regime stability and internal development over displacing the United States as a global military hegemon. Although China’s major, unannounced exercises around Taiwan earlier this month may constitute an exception, overall, Chinese military exercises near Taiwan over the last five years are consistent with this interpretation: many have reacted to perceived provocations, illustrate only medium-scale capabilities, and have generally had a performative quality, accompanied by extensive press coverage.

There is still an opening for the United States and China to de-escalate. To achieve strategic stability, the two countries will need to make a concerted effort to defuse their security dilemma—the dynamic in which each side perceives the other’s defensive measures as aggressive. First, U.S. and Chinese leaders need to revive superpower summitry. Biden held only three face-to-face meetings with Xi on the sidelines of regional economic meetings. Although the May 2026 Beijing summit between Trump and Xi yielded no major breakthroughs, the meeting did improve the two leaders’ personal relationship; today, U.S.-Chinese tensions are lower than they were between 2021 and 2025. This progress suggests the great value of holding a regular, annual, multiday bilateral summit with a significant focus on nuclear arms control. Such meetings would give expert working groups time to methodically develop measures to reduce the risk of conflict. Just as important, the summits need to be long enough to leave room for unscripted conversations. At their first summit, in Geneva in November 1985, U.S. President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev famously broke away from anxious bureaucrats and advisers for an impromptu walk—an encounter that helped establish a more constructive relationship.

The United States must also take concrete steps to reduce the chance of escalation in the Taiwan Strait. Above all, it should adhere more consistently to its “one China” policy—its position that Beijing is the sole legal government of China. More consistency would include limiting U.S. legislators’ trips to the island and downgrading U.S.-Taiwanese defense relations by, for example, holding meetings less frequently and at lower diplomatic levels. Washington should remind key allies such as Japan to proceed cautiously in terms of their rhetoric and military deployments. Such a restraint-oriented strategy would make it clear to Taiwan that independence is off the table, encouraging it to take a more accommodating approach that would lower the temperature with Beijing. If Washington were to agree to common-sense limitations on arms sales to Taiwan—such as refusing to sell Taiwan the surface-to-surface ballistic Army Tactical Missile System (ATACMS), which can reach across the strait to the Chinese mainland—Beijing would likely reciprocate by scaling back its military exercises and related military deployments around the island. There are real incentives for Beijing to de-escalate. Doing so could improve relations with neighbors such as Japan, free up focus for domestic priorities, lower military spending, and limit the chance of war.

The Pentagon needs to demonstrate Washington’s intent to avoid war over Taiwan by gradually decreasing U.S. warship transits through the Taiwan Strait. Even more important, Washington should also substantially reduce U.S. military deployments in the Luzon Strait between Taiwan and the Philippines and around Japan’s Ryukyu Islands. Such deployments only exacerbate the security dilemma.

Exhibiting restraint does not mean the United States would be giving Taiwan away. The United States can continue to provide Taiwan with defensive arms (such as missile interceptors, artillery, drones, and mines) and harden U.S. bases in the region to provide stabilizing deterrence. But even if U.S. leaders publicly abjure direct military intervention to defend Taiwan—a rational step that would lower the risk of nuclear war—China will prefer negotiating with Taipei on the island’s autonomy over a bloody military showdown with Taiwanese forces. For their part, Taiwan’s leaders will likely accommodate themselves to limited self-governance under Chinese overall sovereignty. In the end, China’s main goal is to get Taiwan out of the U.S. sphere of influence. Chinese leaders’ major fear is not so much Taiwanese autonomy as the prospect of the island serving as a U.S. forward base—in Chinese parlance, “using Taiwan to contain China.”

Another important step would be to seek a multilateral pledge by all nuclear-armed states to employ nuclear weapons only in retaliation against a nuclear attack. Such a policy would reduce the risk of miscalculation during a crisis. China has long embraced such a no-first-use policy, but U.S. leaders have traditionally opposed it, believing that it might expose U.S. allies to conventional attack. The U.S. nuclear deterrent for allies, however, increasingly lacks credibility because the costs of starting a nuclear war would vastly outweigh the benefits. And after the collapse of traditional nuclear arms control, a mutual no-first-use policy offers a promising area of common ground between the United States and China. It would reinforce the existing no-first-use policies of China and India and implicitly acknowledge their leadership in the area of nuclear restraint, a virtue when newer nuclear states are chafing under the old Cold War superpowers’ dominance of arms control. This approach could even entice Beijing into a wider, more comprehensive process of bilateral or multilateral nuclear arms control.

Beyond these three major initiatives, the United States and China should sign an agreement to notify each other about their ballistic missile tests. Washington could also consider giving Beijing a larger role in nonproliferation efforts, for instance by affording China leadership roles in negotiations and inspection regimes in future nonproliferation arrangements. The U.S. arms control agenda with China should focus not only on offensive nuclear systems but also on missile defenses and tactical nuclear weapons, as well as AI technologies. And it would help if the United States evolved its own nuclear posture in the direction of restraint by reducing its warheads, warfighting capabilities, and alert posture.

Ultimately, the United States needs to get serious about reining in an arms race with China before its perception that one is apace becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy. The two countries have a mutual interest in restraint. If Washington continues to overlook Beijing’s incentives to compromise—and the real signs that it is willing to do so—an arms race that, as of now, is mostly putative will become a reality. And a catastrophic war that could have been avoided could indeed become inevitable.

#5706. A look at how the Trumps spend their Thanksgiving holiday through the years

Melania Trump delivers a powerful message of gratitude to military families during a visit to Fort Rucker ahead of Thanksgiving. She honors the profound sacrifices made by military spouses and children while their loved ones are deployed across the globe. She expresses deep appreciation for their strength and resilience in keeping their homes full of love.

In keeping with tradition, President Donald Trump marked his sixth Thanksgiving in the executive office with the White House’s annual Turkey Pardon ceremony on Tuesday.

His plans for Thanksgiving Day this year remain unannounced — but previous holidays offer a preview of how the president likes to spend the day honoring those who can't be at home for the uniquely American holiday due to service to the country.

Last year, Trump spent Thanksgiving at Mar-a-Lago participating in his favorite pastime — golf. But he also used the time in what is known as the "Winter White House" to call Maj. Gen. Dave Gardner, commander of the 101st Airborne Division and Joint Task Force–Southern Border, by video conference and talk with troops deployed along the southern border.

TRUMP AND DANA WHITE HONOR MARINE CORPS BAND WITH SIX-FIGURE CHECKS IN FIRST EVENT ON NEW HELIPAD

President Donald Trump delivers remarks to U.S. troops in an unannounced visit to Al Asad Air Base, Iraq, Dec. 26, 2018. (Reuters/Jonathan Ernst)

First lady Melania Trump spent the days ahead of the holiday in 2025 visiting Camp Lejeune and Marine Corps Air Station New River with second lady Usha Vance on Nov. 19. They met with military families and made Thanksgiving crafts with children.

In 2020, during the final Thanksgiving of his first term, Trump remained at the White House and made calls to six deployed military units representing every branch of the armed forces, including troops in Kuwait and sailors aboard the USS Winston Churchill in the Red Sea.

Trump famously took a secret trip to Bagram Airfield in Afghanistan on Nov. 28, 2019, where he served turkey, posed for photos and thanked American troops for their sacrifices amid the ongoing war in the Middle East, which not even two years later, in August 2021, was brought to an end by then-President Joe Biden.

"There's nowhere I'd rather celebrate this Thanksgiving than right here with the toughest, strongest, best, and bravest warriors on the face of the Earth," Trump told the troops at the time.

"And you don't even know how much the people of our country love and respect you."

President Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump greet military personnel during an unannounced visit to Al Asad Air Base, Iraq, Dec. 26, 2018. (Reuters/Jonathan Ernst)

TRUMP SAYS US MAY RECOVER ALL THE EQUIPMENT LEFT BEHIND IN AFGHANISTAN BY BIDEN ADMIN

The visit came as roughly 12,000 American troops remained in Afghanistan more than 18 years after the U.S. invasion.

During the visit, Trump met with Afghan President Ashraf Ghani to discuss efforts to end the war and told American troops that the Taliban wanted to reach a deal with the United States. He said his administration was reducing America's military presence in Afghanistan while pursuing a political solution to the more than 18-year conflict.

President Donald Trump visits with personnel at U.S. Coast Guard Station Lake Worth Inlet in Riviera Beach, Florida, on Thanksgiving Day, Nov. 22, 2018. (Mandel Ngan/AFP via Getty Images)

Trump spent Thanksgiving 2018 in Florida having a traditional dinner with his family, including Melania and his children and grandchildren.

He also held a video call with deployed troops before visiting Coast Guard members at Station Lake Worth Inlet with his wife, where the first couple thanked them for their service and hurricane rescues.

After that holiday in 2018, Melania and then-second lady Karen Pence assembled comfort kits for deployed troops at American Red Cross headquarters.

MOSCOW, TALIBAN FORGE MILITARY ALLIANCE IN POWER GRAB AFTER US AFGHANISTAN EXIT: REPORTS

President Donald Trump speaks to members of the military via teleconference from his Mar-a-Lago resort in Palm Beach, Florida, on Thanksgiving Day, Nov. 22, 2018. (Mandel Ngan/AFP via Getty Images)

Trump spent his first Thanksgiving as president at his Mar-a-Lago estate for a traditional Thanksgiving dinner with his family. It came after a day of video-calling deployed troops.

Donald and Melania Trump also visited Coast Guard Station Lake Worth Inlet in Riviera Beach, Florida, where they handed out food and greeted service members.

Ashley J. DiMella reports on politics for Fox News Digital.

#5704. Trump’s ‘Unprecedented Intervention’ in Nvidia

Q&A: Trump’s ‘Unprecedented Intervention’ in Nvidia

Prefer to listen? To hear this entire conversation, and more episodes in the weeks ahead, follow Ones and Tooze wherever you get your podcasts.

Jensen Huang was reinstated this week as CEO of Nvidia, a semiconductor manufacturer that’s a linchpin of the global artificial intelligence economy. That occurred only after U.S. President Donald Trump personally intervened to persuade Nvidia’s board—despite allegations that Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy, and his efforts to sell Nvidia’s chips to China in contravention of U.S. policy, may have undermined U.S. national security.

Was Huang’s reinstatement initiated by Silicon Valley or D.C. elites? What levers did Trump use to pressure Nvidia’s board? Does Huang, or Nvidia more generally, qualify as “too big to fail”?

Jensen Huang was reinstated this week as CEO of Nvidia, a semiconductor manufacturer that’s a linchpin of the global artificial intelligence economy. That occurred only after U.S. President Donald Trump personally intervened to persuade Nvidia’s board—despite allegations that Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy, and his efforts to sell Nvidia’s chips to China in contravention of U.S. policy, may have undermined U.S. national security.

Was Huang’s reinstatement initiated by Silicon Valley or D.C. elites? What levers did Trump use to pressure Nvidia’s board? Does Huang, or Nvidia more generally, qualify as “too big to fail”?

Those are just a few of the questions that came up in my recent conversation with FP economics columnist Adam Tooze on the podcast we co-host, Ones and Tooze. What follows is an excerpt, edited for length and clarity. For the full conversation, look for Ones and Tooze wherever you get your podcasts. And check out Adam’s Substack newsletter.

Cameron Abadi: Was Huang’s reinstatement initiated by Silicon Valley tech elites or by D.C. political elites—or an entwinement between the two?

Adam Tooze: Some reporting suggests that the rally around Huang really began in Silicon Valley itself. So it was a key group of people who were close to him: Uber founder Travis Kalanick, a bunch of venture capitalists like Gavin Baker, who’s been tweeting very effusively about this, Brad Gerstner and Marc Andreessen, who we’ve discussed on the show before. Heavy hitters. Apparently, there’s some Goldman Sachs interest as well. None of those people have really been willing to comment. But there was a rallying around Jensen Huang and the need to bring him back in. I think, basically, it was a combination of their influence plus a sell-off in the market that really prompted Trump to act. The venture capitalists have good connections to [Vice President] J.D. Vance, because he had that little foray in Silicon Valley finance by way of Peter Thiel. And they seem to then have been able to act on figures inside the Trump administration. Jensen Huang is, after all, very well known to Trump. The two have been seen together a lot in public.

And then there was some last-minute fig leaf-style conversations with the attorney general just to confirm that they’re not actually supporting a figure that is currently under investigation by the American judicial authorities. So apparently the attorney general, Todd Blanche, signed off on this. And that was really then the decisive moment when Trump then intervened with the board, which seems to be a remarkably weak institution. For a company of Nvidia’s size and significance, its corporate governance is schoolyard. It comes out of the era when it was a scrappy manufacturer of accelerator chips for video games rather than the biggest company in the world and the backstop to AI. So it seems to just be this incredible kind of jury-rigged, duct tape—you know, people refer to duct-tape empire—kind of setup that we’re dealing with here. And truly dramatic in its impact then on the market, though questions are being asked, I think, about how long the rebound can really last given the underlying questions about AI and the broader economy.

CA: What are the mechanics by which a leader of the U.S. government overrides a corporate board? And are there any precedents for a U.S. president personally intervening in a boardroom decision like this?

AT: I don’t think he has very many direct levers, other than his public sway. As corporate America has demonstrated across the board during his second term, no one wants to be on his wrong side. So if he told this weak corporate governance body at Nvidia that, you know, this is the way to go, and there really were no legal objections, at least at the level of espionage, then presumably they felt it was in the shareholders’ best interest to just do as they were told. It’s not entirely without precedent.

The most recent instance would be the Obama administration’s move against the leadership of General Motors in the spring of 2009 when the federal government did a bailout for General Motors. And they removed Rick Wagoner, who they didn’t feel that they could work with. Then beyond that, you have to go further back in history to the Cold War-era presidencies. So there’s action by the [Franklin] Roosevelt administration against the Ford Motor Company leadership when they were deeply worried during the wartime about the succession of Henry Ford and deaths within the Ford family. There’s Truman intervening in the steel industry in the early 1950s. There’s a moment when Kennedy also intervenes at U.S. Steel in ’62.

But, you know, the fundamental difference here is that we’re not in a state of war. This is not a matter of urgent national security or of macroeconomic pressure like in the early 1950s during the Korean War. This isn’t the aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis. Nvidia is not on the receiving end of a federal government bailout. You know, the analogies quite rapidly break down and leave one feeling that in some senses, this truly is an unprecedented intervention. This is the most valuable company in the world at various points. And it just basically doesn’t appear to have any serious corporate governance whatsoever.

Jensen Huang and the broader AI sector represent an enormous risk for the entire public.

The return of Nvidia’s Jensen Huang exposes a dangerous gap in corporate oversight.

CA: The intervention on behalf of Jensen Huang seemed to be motivated by a sense that he was somehow essential, not only to the success of the company, but through the company, to the success of the American economy overall. In what sense could Huang be considered to be “too big to fail”?

AT: Well, that term comes out of banking. And within the banking sector, since the Dodd-Frank reforms and other global financial stability reforms in the aftermath of 2008, designations as GSIB, so globally systemically significant banks and financial institutions, are formalized and have been formalized. And they do actually have a relatively formal or quantitative definition. I mean, you can look at bank balance sheets and just trace networks of interconnection and risks that arise from those. And there’s a quite serious study of those kinds of risks. And one could do the same for Nvidia. And there has been a great deal of speculation along these lines, or not just speculation, but investigation. And it’s quite clear that the circular financing mechanisms that we’ve also discussed on the show going back awhile now all center on Nvidia. And so questions have been asked about the stability of the Nvidia financing structure.

But I think the question was always, should they not be subject to some kind of oversight? Right now, there is no risk of failure, right? In some senses this invocation of failure in the worst-case scenario—you know, she’s a spy and Nvidia is going to fail and therefore, you know, we must do x or y, or not do x or y, or bring him back or shove him out or whatever—the whole discourse is massively exaggerated. I mean, they’re a very successful tech business, which right now is in the middle of a boom in AI, which does have some bubble characteristics. But the financing of this is extended and ramified, but it’s the cloud providers, not necessarily Nvidia, that anyone thought of as being immediately in trouble. And even those are some way away from outright failure. And so this, you know, this language of exigency and this language of crisis, you know, it has a historical root and there are some structural reasons why one might worry about Nvidia, but it doesn’t justify the current action one way or the other. And the fact that the company is as poorly structured as it is such that so much revolves around one man is prima-facie reason for, you know, some serious rethinking and some serious structural governance.

But that would require market pressure. And you know, the financial markets right now are bonkers. That they would reprice the company by 30 percent of a trillion dollars on the basis of this kind of news is, in itself, you know, profoundly delegitimizing. So to my mind, like, it’s an absolute disaster of American public discourse, because the allegations appear to be hugely exaggerated, the damage done to the market suggests that the corporate governance is terrible, the reporting by the American media has been shambolic, the president’s intervention is unprecedented and bonkers, and now the markets vindicate the whole thing by raising the value of Nvidia by 30 percent. I mean, it feels like everyone’s kind of lost their minds in some ways. And yet, as someone famously said, whilst the music plays, you dance. Because if you’re not on the Nvidia train, you’re not doing as well as other people. And all of these boosters are saying this is a vindication of the American success story and Jensen Huang is the latest character in that ongoing narrative. It all feels a bit delirious, to be honest.

Cameron Abadi is a deputy editor at Foreign Policy. X: @CameronAbadi

Adam Tooze is a columnist at Foreign Policy and a history professor and the director of the European Institute at Columbia University. He is the author of Chartbook, a newsletter on economics, geopolitics, and history. X: @adam_tooze

With year-end best-of lists about to arrive, one strong contender for film of the year might seem unlikely at first: a five-hour, two-part, largely French-language biopic of French general and statesman Charles de Gaulle that only recently reached U.S. screens. Directed by Antonin Baudry and starring a strikingly de Gaulle-like Simon Abkarian, this French blockbuster comes with an almost-American budget of 74 million euros, one of the largest in the history of francophone cinema. Perhaps unsurprisingly given its subject, it became the hit of the French summer, offering audiences a nostalgic vision of national greatness at a moment of paralysis and division.

More surprisingly, the de Gaulle diptych has won praise outside of France as well, helped by the fact that it works superbly as both action and entertainment. Epic in scale, beautifully shot, both wryly amusing and often touching, its twin installments pass far more quickly than their daunting runtime might suggest. There are clear contemporary echoes, too, in de Gaulle’s personal struggles and story of dogged European defiance. Indeed, it is not hard to see why viewers in France and elsewhere have warmed to this tale of an embattled European leader fighting to re-build sovereignty in the face of pressure from the United States as the moorings of a crumbling old order give way to something frightening and new.

With year-end best-of lists about to arrive, one strong contender for film of the year might seem unlikely at first: a five-hour, two-part, largely French-language biopic of French general and statesman Charles de Gaulle that only recently reached U.S. screens. Directed by Antonin Baudry and starring a strikingly de Gaulle-like Simon Abkarian, this French blockbuster comes with an almost-American budget of 74 million euros, one of the largest in the history of francophone cinema. Perhaps unsurprisingly given its subject, it became the hit of the French summer, offering audiences a nostalgic vision of national greatness at a moment of paralysis and division.

More surprisingly, the de Gaulle diptych has won praise outside of France as well, helped by the fact that it works superbly as both action and entertainment. Epic in scale, beautifully shot, both wryly amusing and often touching, its twin installments pass far more quickly than their daunting runtime might suggest. There are clear contemporary echoes, too, in de Gaulle’s personal struggles and story of dogged European defiance. Indeed, it is not hard to see why viewers in France and elsewhere have warmed to this tale of an embattled European leader fighting to re-build sovereignty in the face of pressure from the United States as the moorings of a crumbling old order give way to something frightening and new.

Each of the film’s two parts is just over two and a half hours long. The first, De Gaulle: Résistance (158 minutes; released in France as L’Age de fer), opens with the humiliation of the French collapse in June 1940. Refusing to accept the armistice, de Gaulle flees to England in a tiny plane. From there, he presses British Prime Minister Winston Churchill for greater support and builds a shaky government-in-exile from scratch, operating from a tiny office in central London.

The second, De Gaulle: Liberté (159 minutes; J’écris ton nom in France), covers 1943 to the end of 1944, following both the actions of the Resistance and de Gaulle’s power struggles with rival claimants to French leadership, before moving on to D-Day and the liberation of Paris. The epic closes movingly on Armistice Day, when Churchill visits the freed capital as de Gaulle’s guest.

For audiences outside France, some of this will be familiar, from de Gaulle’s defiant broadcasts on the BBC to his haughty and stubborn personal affect. Undeniably imperious and quite unable to forget a slight, Abkarian’s de Gaulle is both a model of determination in the face adversity and, to the Allied leaders who bankrolled him, a quintessentially French pain in the ass.

A still from De Gaulle: Résistance.Pathe Films

Other episodes are less well known in the English-speaking world, however, even as they remain central to France’s own story of the war, from the British destruction of the French fleet at Mers-el-Kébir in July 1940 (to keep its warships out of German hands) to the epic battle at Bir Hakeim in mid-1942. Perhaps now more familiar to tourists as the name of a Paris metro station, Bir Hakeim saw 3,700 Free French soldiers and their African colonial troops hold an isolated desert fort in Libya against German Gen. Erwin Rommel’s Afrika Korps for more than two weeks. Fighting against overwhelming odds, their bravery allowed Britain’s Eighth Army to fall back to El Alamein and regroup, marking an eventual turning point in the wider war. Providing the first film with a dramatic 15-minute denouement, the battle proved that de Gaulle’s ragtag movement could fight as a real army, provided a much-needed fillip to Free French morale, and strengthened the general’s position as a legitimate and potentially successful French leader.

Although this is very much a big-budget war movie, much of its power lies, paradoxically, in its intimate portrayal of the quiet complexities of leadership. In the public mind, de Gaulle can often come across as a cartoonish figure, all stubborn resolve, frosty self-regard, and Gallic hauteur. Abkarian’s ramrod-stiff performance is magnetic and provides plenty of evidence of this. But it also offers something more human, portraying with affection de Gaulle’s strange mix of grandeur and loneliness. The first film dwells in particular on his isolation and frequent despair. Arriving in London as a defeated tank division commander and former undersecretary of war, de Gaulle has no army, no money, barely any staff, and little claim to legitimate leadership. His situation is often tragi-comic, as when he tries unsuccessfully to win over members of the French expatriate community at a drinks party, or when he attempts to address a British audience in a packed theater, only to walk off ashamed without saying a word. In one especially memorable scene, he weeps alone in the bath of his small, dingy flat. In many others he is disconsolate, close to losing hope, and tempted to give up.

This most Gallic of films is in fact based on an equally epic book by a British academic: A Certain Idea of France, Julian Jackson’s 900-page biography, published in 2018. Reviewing it in the New Yorker, Adam Gopnik dwelt on the crippling weakness de Gaulle faced in 1940, and how he ultimately managed to think his way out of it via a mixture of imagination, self-belief, and obstinacy. De Gaulle depended “more on theatrical élan than did pretty much any other public man of his century,” as Gopnik put it. “No one has ever played a weaker hand more compellingly. His life was one long brilliant bluff.”

It is this vulnerability, rather than the more familiar image of pigheaded strength, that likely appealed to French audiences, prompting a reassessment of his traditionally unbending image and the controversial Gaullist legacy it inspired. For all that, the film is also huge fun. Its action sequences are slickly executed and, unusually for a European production, come with plenty of exuberant, Hollywood-style explosions. But it works as entertainment above all because at its center is the double act of de Gaulle and Churchill, played by Simon Russell Beale, easily the best of the many actors who have attempted the role.

A still from De Gaulle: Liberté.Pathe Films

The two men are endlessly frustrated by one another and an obvious study in contrasts: one reserved, austere, and abstemious, the other impulsive, theatrical, and alcoholic. Yet each recognizes in the other a wartime leader fighting to save his nation against massive odds, creating a certain fondness and clear mutual regard. Among their many fine scenes is a comic row involving translation. De Gaulle speaks poor English; Churchill’s French is comical but serviceable. As they argue, both men hear their respective interpreters diplomatically softening their words. Each leader throws his man out of the room in turn, preferring to fight out their differences in broken language. The grudging but sincere warmth between the two both humanizes the complexities of wartime leadership and provides the film’s emotional heart.

Some critics have accused director Baudry of playing fast and loose with history, mixing invented characters with historical leaders, among other sins against accuracy. Jackson, who acted as a consultant on the production, has written warmly in its defense: “My pavlovian historical pedantry – ‘no that is wrong, it didn’t happen like that’, ‘you have these events in the wrong order’, etc – was quickly slapped down with the reminder that this was a film not a documentary.”

The film’s very French portrayal of the United States, with a Machiavellian President Franklin D. Roosevelt cast as a chief villain, is one obvious area of potential historical dispute. But it also provides the film with its drama. Curiously, Adolf Hitler is never seen and barely even mentioned, while few German soldiers even appear. Instead, the real antagonist is Roosevelt’s Washington, and the U.S. president’s mounting frustration with an upstart French exile who contributes little manpower to the war effort yet irritatingly demands to be treated as an equal and a great power. In this sense it has something in common with zombie movies, where the greatest danger often comes less from the outside menace and more from potential betrayal within the group of humans struggling to survive.

A still from De Gaulle: Liberté.Pathe Films

In Roosevelt’s eyes, France had forfeited any claim to great-power status, while de Gaulle himself was merely an arrogant annoyance and obstacle to his plans. This broader threat to French survival is embodied in a plan to create the Allied Military Government of Occupied Territories (AMGOT), which the film presents as a U.S. scheme to permanently dismantle and divide the country. In this vision, a liberated France would be run by U.S. and British administrators, much as occupied Germany later was. That AMGOT was never the fully formed plan for France the film suggests is almost beside the point. In one memorable scene, Churchill is shown a future map of Europe in which France has vanished, carved up into a “New Wallonia” and other invented entities. In an act of covert friendship, he leaks it to de Gaulle; a rare act of British solidarity with the French over the Americans.

As exaggerated as the film’s version of the AMGOT plan may be—and Jackson concedes it is somewhat overplayed—the question of how to deal with a powerful United States runs throughout the film, giving it its most obvious modern resonance. In part this reflects a traditional and enduring Franco-British divide, with France seeking self-sufficiency and sovereignty while Britain prefers proximity and access to Washington.

To distract from runaway protests, the French president is making a show of independence on the world stage.

The film’s ideas have poisoned military thinking for centuries.

On the eve of D-Day in June 1944, for instance, de Gaulle’s demands over his forces’ role in the coming liberation of France prompt another giant bust-up with Churchill, and one especially memorable exchange, recounted in de Gaulle’s own highly readable memoirs. “”Every time we have to choose between Europe and the open seas, we shall always choose the open seas,”” he recalls Churchill declaring. “”Every time I have to choose between you and Roosevelt, I shall always choose Roosevelt.”” From Churchill’s point of view, this was entirely sensible; Britain had no obvious alternative to a superpower’s existential support, and it would have been foolish to side with an exile liberation army possessing no resources of its own. Nonetheless, it was a line de Gaulle would go on to quote throughout his life: an emblem of British perfidy and deference to Washington.

Late in the second film, in a scene set in November 1944, de Gaulle sounds out Churchill on a deeper Anglo-French alliance. Churchill declines because Britain must stay close to Washington. The portrayal feels both enduring but also clearly modern, depicting two exhausted European powers facing common adversity but still quite unable to choose to be full partners with one another.

More than anything, the film brings to mind the modern predicament of embattled and weakened middle powers, trying to find their way in a world dominated by far larger and more chaotic forces. During World War II, Britain and France both still thought of themselves as great powers—in de Gaulle’s case almost absurdly so, given his limited circumstances. Yet both clearly lived at the mercy of others, be they Hitler’s marauding armies or the caprice of an indispensable but overbearing U.S. ally.

Today European nations face a version of the same bind, struggling to rebuild sovereignty in a world dominated by superpowers increasingly willing to coerce and threaten them. The message of the film is clearly a comfortable one for French audiences: France was right all along about untrustworthy Americans, and about the need for strength and independence rather than reliance on potentially unreliable U.S.-led institutions like NATO. Nonetheless, here de Gaulle offers modern Europeans clear lessons on how to counteract weakness, via a mixture of political imagination, risk-taking, and—above all—a willingness to stand up to U.S. power from time to time.

What most people understand as “Gaullist” policies are increasingly common far beyond France as our geopolitical order frays, not least intrusive industrial policies aimed at technological self-sufficiency. Ben Judah, a British author and former political advisor, has gone further, proposing a new agenda of “Anglo-Gaullism” inspired by the French leader’s mixture of interventionism and political élan. “[T]he genius of de Gaulle was to re-enchant through storytelling a nation that had utterly lost confidence in itself,” he writes. Europe could clearly use a little more of that Gaullist enchantment today.

It is almost a cliche to contrast the giants of World War II with the slighter figures of our own generation. Yet watching de Gaulle’s struggles, it is hard not to think of the supplication of modern leaders like Mark Rutte, NATO’s secretary-general, whose approach to U.S. President Donald Trump was memorably described by Susan Glasser of the New Yorker as “strategic self-abasement.” De Gaulle is often fairly criticized for a grandiose vision of French leadership that far outstripped France’s actual power, leading to unhelpful delusions of national grandeur fed by the vision of its grandest of leaders. Nonetheless, de Gaulle’s obdurate refusal to accept decline—and his determination that France should stand, as he put it, as a nation “in the front rank”—should serve as an inspiration to Europe’s leaders today. This, too, is the lesson of the two excellent films that bear his name: to hold a vision of national power and to will it obstinately into existence, even if only by learning how to play a bad hand well.

#5701. Why Israel Is Losing America

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

ANDREW P. MILLER is a Senior Fellow in National Security and International Policy at the Center for American Progress. He was Deputy Assistant Secretary of State for Israeli-Palestinian Affairs in the Biden administration and Director for Egypt and Israel Military Issues on the National Security Council in the Obama administration.

Only a Radical Course Change Can Win Back Its Most Important Ally

American politicians have woken up to the fact that the public has soured on Israel. On November 3, as Americans headed to the polls, U.S. President Donald Trump made the surprising announcement that the United States would stop sending aid to Israel, valued at around $4 billion annually, by the end of the year. That night, Democrats, many of whom are increasingly outspoken in their criticism of Israeli actions, swept the House and Senate.

As I wrote in Foreign Affairs a year ago, the “exceptional relationship” between the United States and Israel, in which Israel is treated differently than any other U.S. ally or partner, is coming to an end. No other country receives the tremendous latitude and unconditional backing that the United States extends to Israel. In addition to directly hurting Palestinians, the United States’ support for Israel incentivizes reckless Israeli behavior and dubious strategic thinking. The consequences of the blank check are clear. Over the past three years, tens of thousands of Gazans have been killed, progress toward peace and reconstruction in the Gaza Strip has stalled, the annexation of the West Bank proceeds at an unprecedented rate, and the United States is stuck in an unpopular war in the Middle East with seemingly no end. Israel, for its part, is no safer than on October 6, 2023, and unquestionably more isolated.

Things are about to change. For better or worse, the United States will recalibrate its relationship with Israel over the coming years and a new paradigm for the bilateral relationship will emerge—one in which Israel is expected to comply with U.S. and international law, the two countries refrain from interfering in each other’s domestic politics, and the United States limits its support when Israeli goals conflict with its own.

This change is inevitable, and there is little that Israel and its supporters can do to stop it. But Israel can help keep the United States onside by making itself a reliable partner. As it begins what could be a drawn-out government formation process after last month’s elections, Israel can opt to change direction and plot a course that will not further alienate its closest ally.

Whoever leads the next Israeli government can begin rebuilding trust with the United States before a new U.S. president takes office, in 2029. It won’t be easy. Just as Americans have grown critical of Israel over the past three years, Israelis have shifted further to the right. Israel’s next leaders will need the courage to curb the country’s expansionist policies and resurrect the much-maligned two-state solution. But if they fail to overhaul their approach to Palestinians and the wider region, Israel risks losing its biggest champion and defender—perhaps for good.

Trump, who seems to delight in bullying U.S. allies and partners, has maintained the United States’ long-standing exceptional approach to Israel. He joined Israel in launching strikes on Iran in June 2025 and a larger war in February 2026, embarking for the first time on a truly joint military operation with the Jewish state. Like other presidents before him, Trump has provided Israel with bombs, missiles, and aircraft, largely with no strings attached. He and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have also interfered in each other’s political systems to an unprecedented degree by endorsing candidates.

Time and again, Trump has deferred to Israel even when such support has run against American interests. The 2026 war on Iran is the most blatant example. Netanyahu persuaded Trump to give up nuclear talks with Iran and join a war that has failed in its objectives and upended energy markets. Even where the Trump administration has staked out U.S. priorities, it has largely refrained from trying to compel Israel to adhere to them. Israel, for example, has obstructed Trump’s peace plan for Gaza, which is meant to restore governance to the Palestinians, disarm Hamas, and lead to a permanent Israeli withdrawal from the territory. Israel has undermined the plan by expanding its military footprint in Gaza beyond the agreed demarcation lines and denying entry to the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG), an interim technocratic body that is intended to govern the territory under Trump’s plan and is currently marooned in Egypt. But the Trump administration has barely sounded a single note of disapproval, reinforcing Netanyahu’s long-standing view that he can defy the United States at little cost.

Moreover, it remains to be seen whether Trump will follow through on his pledge to cut military aid to Israel. The timing of his statement suggests it could have been an electoral stunt, and he said himself that the announcement would deprive the left of a talking point. One possibility is that the United States continues gifting Israel weapons to the tune of billions, just under a different guise. The National Defense Authorization Act for fiscal year 2027, which passed the House this summer and could pass the Senate before Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress this coming January, contains a provision that would expand the Pentagon’s financial and material assistance to Israel.

Trump has made no effort to bring U.S. military assistance or transfers to Israel in line with what it provides to other countries. For decades, the United States has been reluctant to subject arms sales to Israel to U.S. regulations or condition them on Israeli behavior. All recent presidents, for example, have effectively exempted Israel from so-called Leahy laws, which prohibit U.S. assistance to foreign military units credibly implicated in human-rights violations. Despite rampant settler terrorism in the West Bank, in many cases facilitated by the Israeli military, the Trump administration has not indicated that it would declare any Israeli units ineligible to receive U.S. weapons.

Trump has also intervened in Israeli politics more than any other U.S. leader. He has hectored Israeli President Isaac Herzog to pardon Netanyahu so that the prime minister can escape the consequences of an ongoing corruption trial. Ahead of October’s election in Israel, Trump offered Netanyahu a “complete and total endorsement” in his bid for another term. Such blatant interference in Israel’s domestic politics not only undermines the rule of law and integrity of Israeli elections but also serves to normalize Netanyahu’s repeated interventions in U.S. domestic politics. True to form, the Israeli prime minister has praised Trump as “by far the greatest friend Israel has ever had or will have in the White House” just two weeks before the U.S. midterm elections, effectively endorsing Republican candidates for Congress. As in other areas of the relationship, Trump has made what is already an unhealthy dynamic worse.

Unconditional support from the United States has hurt Israel in a crucial way: it indulges the worst instincts of Israeli leaders and does nothing to dissuade them from their embrace of a near-perpetual state of war. After Hamas’s attack three years ago, Israel has bombed Gaza, Iran, Lebanon, Syria, Yemen, and even Qatar. Although Israel has dealt blows to its adversaries, there is no evidence that these wars have made Israel any safer. Iran and its proxies have been weakened, but in the course of fighting, Tehran has discovered the extent of its leverage over the Strait of Hormuz and the global economy and appears even more interested in developing a nuclear weapon. In Lebanon, Hezbollah still poses a threat and is devising new ways of striking Israeli territory. Although confined to a smaller portion of Gaza, Hamas is reconstituting its capabilities and quashing any internal Palestinian challenge to its rule. And in the West Bank, runaway settler violence, the proliferation of illegal Israeli outposts, and the growing threat of terrorism or even a Palestinian uprising have pushed the territory to the breaking point.

Israel has also drifted ever closer to pariah status, isolated internationally thanks to its aggressive tactics. Even the country’s closest historical allies have imposed punitive measures that would have been unthinkable just five years ago. Canada, France, and the United Kingdom, for example, announced wide-ranging sanctions against Israeli settlements in the West Bank in September. Such policies are no longer only the purview of traditional critics of Israel, such as Indonesia and Ireland.

Israel’s reputation within the United States has also tanked. According to Pew polling, 60 percent of Americans have an unfavorable view of Israel, up from 42 percent in 2022. So far, Trump has stopped Congress from restricting support for Israel—both through threatening vetoes and applying pressure on congressional Republicans—but he cannot hold back the tide of American public opinion indefinitely. Once it breaks, Israelis will have to face more than criticism from its closest ally and security guarantor. With Democrats soon to be in control of both the House and the Senate, Congress will likely pass bills that sanction settlement building and condition military aid on adherence to U.S. and international law.

Without changes in U.S. and Israeli policy, the two countries could see their relationship rupture as continued support for Israel becomes politically untenable in the United States. To rehabilitate itself in the eyes of Americans—and therefore ensure long-term cooperation with the United States—Israel will need to change course. It must abandon Netanyahu’s bludgeoning approach to both the Palestinians and the wider region.

It is no exaggeration to say that the future of the U.S.-Israeli relationship rests on what type of government Israel forms in the next few months. Netanyahu’s exclusion from the next government represents the best hope for preserving bilateral relations with the United States. Netanyahu has proved unwilling to stay out of U.S. politics or modify draconian security policies that have run afoul of the American public. Unfortunately, most of Netanyahu’s rivals for prime minister share his hawkish position on the Palestinians and the Middle East. Were they in power, they seem likely to resist fundamental revisions to Israeli policy that could safeguard the bilateral relationship.

Israel’s next leaders need to journey outside their comfort zone. They will have to come to terms with new realities: that tensions between the United States and Israel are now deep-rooted and that they can’t rely on the adamantine support of the Republican party any longer. To win back Americans, the Israeli government will have to rigorously follow through on its commitments under Trump’s plan for Gaza, daring Hamas to follow suit. In addition to flooding Gaza with humanitarian aid, Israel should let the NCAG enter the territory to offer an alternative to Hamas’s rule and nihilistic agenda. Enabling the deployment of newly trained Palestinian security forces and the formation of the International Stabilization Force, a peacekeeping mission, would also help show that, whatever unfolds in Gaza, Israel is operating in good faith. Israeli forces should immediately return to the demarcation lines traced in Trump’s Gaza peace plan and pull back even further in concert with Hamas’s progress in fulfilling the terms of the plan until Israel has completely withdrawn from Gaza.

Israel must also rein in violent settlers in the West Bank and hold them accountable through the courts. The Israeli security services can identify the leaders and primary instigators behind the violence and should arrest them and bring them to justice. Given that settlers have killed and injured American citizens in these attacks, continued inaction by Israeli authorities is a recipe for more friction with the United States, especially if a Democratic government comes to power in Washington.

Israel must also halt its creeping annexation of the West Bank. Over the past three years, the Netanyahu government has increased its military presence in the West Bank, deprived the Palestinian Authority of funds, asserted Israeli government control over larger swaths of Palestinian land, approved a slew of new Israeli settlements, and retroactively legalized illicit outposts. In sum, these actions aim to render a Palestinian state impossible. Although reversing these measures would not arrest the expansion of existing settlements and Israeli infrastructure throughout the West Bank, they would be received positively in the United States.

Israeli leaders also need to break the taboo around Palestinian statehood. Only a couple of decades ago, the idea of a Palestinian state was conceivable to most Israelis. Today, Israeli politicians, with precious few exceptions, cannot bring themselves to endorse a two-state solution. It will take time and no small degree of political resolve, but Israeli leaders must convince the public to accept the necessity and the virtues of a Palestinian state existing side by side with Israel. An Israel that can view Palestinians as neighbors entitled to the same rights would provide a very different image to the world than a messianic government bent on expelling whole populations.

These steps will not satisfy all American critics of Israel. Anti-Israeli attitudes cannot be erased in a matter of months. Where anti-Israeli opinion intersects with anti-Semitism—evident in incidents such as a recent boycott of Jewish-owned restaurants in Philadelphia organized by the group Philly Bike on Your Left—the task is even more difficult and will necessitate a different set of policies that transcend Israel, including the formation of diverse domestic and international coalitions to identify and condemn anti-Semitic acts. Yet a far less belligerent Israel and one newly committed to the resolution of the unanswered question of Palestinian self-determination would start to shift U.S. public opinion back in the country’s favor.

If Israel fails to change course, it will find itself less secure and more isolated internationally. Without access to international markets and capital, its economy, which has withstood the turmoil of the last several years remarkably well, will suffer and living standards will fall. Under these circumstances, Jewish Israeli citizens with second passports may elect to leave, depriving the state of its raison d’être—providing a safe and prosperous homeland for the Jewish people. Put simply, an Israel without American support will struggle to survive.

#5700. German Culture Could Soon Be Officially Anti-German

Dispatch: German Culture Could Soon Be Officially Anti-German
